These questions are aimed at Ken Lill, but I am asking them in a public forum in case anyone else thinks of any questions to ask about Ken's "Blue Ram Operating Guide," a tutorial that Ken created that teaches a user how to use the Blue Ram hardware and shows the new functions of Blue Ram BASIC.

I began working on creating the "Blue Ram Operating Guide" video yesterday.  This will eventually make its way to YouTube, hopefully, this week with commentary and additional pictures at the beginning of the video.  I have some questions about the "Guide" that I hope Ken can answer:

1) I recorded version 1.0 of the "Guide."  It is made up of four loads.  How large is each load?  Is it 16K?  If so, does that mean the full program is 64K long?

2) If I HALT the "Guide" to LIST it, then how do I LIST all of it?  I ask this because I think that LIST in BRB only lists the normal 4K of RAM.  Is that right?

3) I could no get the 5-load version of Blue Ram Operating Guide 1.1 to load properly.  It seems that load 2 and 3 are identical.  Is this an archiving error, or is version 1.1 of the program unfinished?

4) In Paul's archive notes he says that version 1.1 "includes a brief introductory
part not found in version 1.0."  Are there any other differences between the two different versions of the "Guide?"  Was version 1.1 distributed.

5) Paul notes that it took about three months to write the "Guide."  Ken, did you work on this program on a daily basis?

6) What tools did you use to write the "Guide?"  Did you use the Blue Ram keyboard to type the program into the Astrocade?

7)  Did you make printouts of the "Guide" to work from so that you didn't have to work from the screen?

8) Did Perkins Engineering know that you were writing the "Guide," or did you finish it up and then just send it to them?  It was eventually included on a tape the later Blue Ram owners got, right?  What tape was the "Guide" included on when it did ship?

9) Did you get any feedback from Blue Ram users about the "Guide."

I'd like to include information like this in the "Guide" video.  Ken, if there is any other information that you can think of about the creation of the "Guide" would be useful background, then I'd like to include that in the video too.

Adam
15501:
OK! Let's start out by saying Yes, I did use a Blue Ram keyboard.
Now to the technical stuff. I don't remember writing a second version.
It was written entirely on a 16K BR unit using BRB 1.1
There are quite a few redundancies between the loads.

The "sense" line, that looks for the input signal is basically the same.
The save lines are identical.
The working Basic program can be listed in it's entirety. However, there are some tricks to list the area that loads the sections in.
It probably would've fit onto a 32K unit except for all of the pictures (SHOWs). They are loaded into the 6&7Kh areas, while the program starts @ !8000.
I did work on this as much as I could after work during the 3 months. The guide I had was Perkins Engineering Blue Ram Basic 1.1 operating guide that came with the original unit, and a lot of conferring with John and Clyde Perkins (both deceased).
I don't remember what was on the other side, but I do know that they shipped with all units starting about 6 month after I finished. It saved a lot of trees!
The only feedback I initially received was from John and Clyde, Mike White, Don Gladden and Dave Carson. All positive. Sadly, I don't know if Don is still alive, but Mike White is the only one I know of that is alive.
BRB 1.1 will list the program that is located in the areas defined by 2 addresses:  %(!6FFC) and %(!6C82)%(!6FFC) is the beginning of the program area and %(!6C82) defines 2 bytes after the last byte of the program.%(!6FFE) defines where the last  available program address is located.
When you stop the running BRB Guide program, %(!6FFC) S/B !8000 and %(!6FFE)  S/B !A072.
If you are trying to PRINT the program to a printer, you will need a parallel port, Centronics printer and the hardware that goes to the Blue Ram ZIF socket. Also the cable that goes with between them.

https://archive.org/details/BlueRamOperatingGuidebyKenLill


I also posted about this "Guide" video on AtariAge, here:


http://atariage.com/forums/topic/279045-added-video-for-astrocades-blue-ram-operating-guide/


The Blue Ram Operating Guide by Ken Lill is a Blue Ram BASIC tutorial written for the Bally Arcade/ Astrocade in 1984.


The Blue Ram Operating Guide loads using the Perkins Engineering Blue Ram RAM expansion for the Bally Arcade/Astrocade.  The "Guide" is an interactive tutorial which starts out explaining the operation of the Blue Ram hardware-- how to connect it to the Astrocade, what the switches do, and more.  This includes some images and animations.  The later sections are mostly text explaining the new commands in Blue Ram BASIC.


The Blue Ram Operating Guide requires 16K of expansion RAM and is used from four cassette tape loads (actually, each load is three separate loads).  When the load is done, it tells the user to turn off the tape (i.e. stop playing the archived file).  It also tells the user when to turn the tape back on again.  Then the program automatically senses when the new load is started.  It then asks the user to wait for the load and then goes through its explanation again.

It took Ken Lill over three months to create the tape that shows almost all of the features of the Blue Ram BASIC 1.1 in "real time."  The tutorial actually shows on the screen what each feature does and how to use it, rather than the user needing to go through the manual and look up how the new Blue Ram BASIC commands work.

The video is split into three main parts:

0:00 - Narration and overview of Blue Ram Operating Guide
7:40 - Blue Ram Operating Guide (video of all four parts of the tutorial)
37:21 - End Credits

If you're curious about the extra features of Blue Ram BASIC 1.1, then you will enjoy this tutorial for Astrocade users.  This video makes a great follow-up to the overview that I made of the Blue Ram hardware last week.  If you missed that video, then you can read about it in this post:


http://atariage.com/forums/topic/278894-blue-ram-expansion-for-astrocade-hardware-overview/


The Blue Ram hardware is a mystery to many Astrocade fans.  Hopefully this video helps to shed some light on this otherwise niche area of the Astrocade that few have seen before now.

The System

The Datamax UV-1R Zgrass Graphics System is a highly interactive, dedicated micro-computer color graphics system designed to easily produce visuals in motion. The UV-1R (University Version 1 Rack-mount) hardware is Z80 microprocessor-based. The Zgrass (Z80 GRAphics Symbiosis System) software is both a high-level computer graphics language and a sophisticated operating system. The EPROM (Erasable Programmable Read Only Memory) firmware houses Zgrass and allows for easy software updates. The system's heritage derives from video arcade games, and the high-speed animation "tricks" so easily programmed on this computer are a result of the development of video game technology and custom video chips.

The Operator's Manual & Supporting Documentation

The Datamax UV-1R Zgrass Graphics System Operator's Manual has been designed to function not only as a guide for initial set up of the system, but also as a reference manual useful during routine operation of the system.

The TABLE OF CONTENTS doubles as a QUICK REFERENCE section, listing ail section headings. Detailed instructions, descriptions, and appropriate illustrations are presented in the body of the manual to guide the user. The TROUBLESHOOTING section provides tips for solving problems. The INDEX OF SYSTEM TESTS locates all the testing programs (macros) contained within the body of the manual and explains how to use the UTILITY DISK to load and run these tests.

References are made throughout this manual to the following additional supporting documentation of the system:

The Datamax UV-1R Zgrass Lessons - The lessons were designed to aid the interested novice in learning how to control the system and create useful custom software.

The Datamax UV-1R Zgrass Glossary - The glossary defines and demonstrates commands and terms necessary tor the use of the Zgrass language.

This manual instructs you on the set-up and testing of the computer and connection of peripheral devices. In addition, it provides you with important information about operating the system... such as, the hardware features and specifications; basic disk and audio tape management techniques; graphic considerations; etc.

The included chapters are:

1 - Introduction
2 - Hardware Features
3 - Initial Set Up
4 - System Power-Up
5 - UV-1R ZGRASS Graphics System Configuration
6 - Peripheral Device Configuration
7 - Troubleshooting
8 - Index of System Tests

Just wanted to throw in some updates on Astrocade dev tools I've been working on...



I've released the first version of astroimg, a little Python script that takes any image and converts it to ready-to-compile Astrocade source code. The script actually produces two files--the ROM itself, which simply displays the graphic, and a separate .gfx file that contains the raw graphic data. One cool feature is that it optimizes for the Astrocade's 8-color palette by determining the best place to position the horizontal color boundary, creating separate palettes for each half of the image, then putting that boundary and palette into the resulting ROM. Here's an example:


[thegif.gif]<http://atariage.com/forums/uploads/monthly_05_2018/post-62680-0-26718400-1527636087.gif>

This image isn't the best, in part because I used a webcam photo with poor lighting and a messy studio behind me. And in the real world, you would probably choose a softer color palette than the bright red and magenta shown here. But hopefully you get the idea. You can also dither the image by passing in a --dither flag at the command line. If you're comfortable running Python scripts without an accompanying instruction guide, you can grab the tool at https://github.com/h.../tools/astroimg<https://github.com/hxlnt/astrocade/tree/master/tools/astroimg>. The code works OK, but it's in serious need of some refactoring, so that's what's next for me. I wrote it all in about 2 nights, so it definitely looks like frenzied-girl-at-a-hackathon code. I may also try to do some smart resizing/cropping, as right now the script just squashes everything to 160x102 regardless of the image's original aspect ratio.

I'd like to eventually make astroimg interoperable with my astropaint tool<https://rawgit.com/hxlnt/astrocade/master/tools/astropaint/index.html> so that you can convert an image, upload it into astropaint, and tweak it by hand. Instead of doing that useful work this weekend, I used astropaint to sketch out an adventure game title screen instead...

[Screen Shot 2018-05-28 at 9.17.07 PM.png]<http://atariage.com/forums/uploads/monthly_05_2018/post-62680-0-38773900-1527636823.png>

Additionally, I posted another demo on GitHub. You may recognize it as a shameless ripoff of tribute to the COLOR PICK demo, but refactored to dynamically adjust the horizontal color boundary.

[Screen Shot 2018-05-29 at 5.52.13 PM.png]<http://atariage.com/forums/uploads/monthly_05_2018/post-62680-0-10462000-1527636800.png>

I've been thinking about making a music composition tool next. Or a Bally BASIC WAV generator. (Does such a thing exist already?)

OK, that's all for now. Let me know if you end up finding any of this stuff useful!  [;)]

I added a Viper Update Letter to BallyAlley.com.  This letter is from Alternative Engineering and it is dated October 1, 1982.


This two-page letter to "All Bally/Astrocade Owners" has new products announcements and prices for Bally Arcade / Astrocade Viper System 5, Viper System Keyboard, System 1 Board Kit and Vipersoft BASIC. The products are described and prices are given for both assembled products and kits that users can build themselves.

A cartridge is announced here call Vipersoft BASIC Operating System.  It seems to be (or would have been?) Vipersoft BASIC on a cartidge with a built-in tape interface.

You can read the letter here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/viper/viper.html#ViperSystemPamphlet



Thanks once more to Michael Matte for sending me this letter.  It's a real treat to see "new" information like this documentation.

[cid:7b1260a1-5e4b-4bb1-8aa5-4535b2b1d555]

If you'd like to see these pictures running in MAME, then here are the eight 4K binary files ("cartridges").  These have been zipped into one file:


http://atariage.com/forums/index.php?app=core&module=attach&section=attach&attach_id=576598


(If the above link doesn't work, then see the thread for a link that probably should work better.)


These pictures on the Astrocade seem to be in only two colors.  I was hoping that there could be black, white and two different grays to make the image a little smoother, but for whatever reason Pillow, as used by AstroImg, didn't provide this in the final picture.  Too, bad, this might have looked much better.


Here is an overview of the way I created each Astrocade image:

  1.  Took a screenshot of "Bad Apple" running under VLC.
  2.  Cropped the screenshot with Photoshop CS2 to 160x101 pixels (w=1.666, H=1.052 and Resolution=96.12)
  3.  Saved the cropped image as an RGB PNG.  I did NOT reduce the colors manually.
  4.  Converted the PNG to a Z80/Gfx using AstroImg.
  5.  Assembled the resulting z80 source code using the Zmac assembler.
  6.  Ran the resulting binary as a cartridge in MAME.

I'd love to see what other users can create using the new AstroImg utility for the Astrocade!  Maybe we can start a new thread with our image results.  Let's see what a system that can only push 160x102 pixels can do nearly automatically when using AstroImg!

I added an "AstroBASIC" version of the Color Organ/Light Show Demo by L&M Software. This is the September 1980 Bally BASIC version that has been saved in "AstroBASIC's" 2000-baud format. This program was designed to work with the L&M interface unit, which probably plugged into hand controller ports 2 and 4. Moving the knobs on those two controllers has the effect of simulating (to a limited extent) the "stereo" input that the stereo hardware interface would have allowed.

You can download the program here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/l&m_software/l&m_software.html#ColorOrganLandMSoftwareAB


Here is some additional information about L&M Software's 1980 Color Organ/Light Show Demo:

This program was designed to work with the L&M interface Unit. According to the FAQ, "Interface Bally to any stereo amp with audio power 1 watt on up. TV displays in step with your stereo music." Even without it, it still displays various graphical effects (kind of like a screen saver). Another program simply labeled "Light Show Demo." is quite similar, but the menu has a few different effects.

From L&M's Software full-page ad in the Arcadian:

Stereo color organ, light show on your TV, Interface with Bally
Opto-Isolated / All Colors / Brilliant Display
Color Organ/Light Show: Interface Bally to any stereo amplifier with audio power of 1 watt on up. Will not affect stereo quality. TV displays in step with your stereo music. Complete interface unit with cassette demonstration program and instructions. $29.95. Add your own Favorite Art/Graphics, etc.

I examined this program's BASIC code. The program is looking for input from the knobs on the hand controllers in ports #2 and #4. It seems that knob #2 acts as the stereo's right channel and that knob #4 is the left channel. Although I've never seen the hardware or the instructions for Color Organ, I now presume that the hardware is a small box that plugs into ports 2 and 4. The volume levels that come into the box are changed to knob values between -128 to 127 (-128 is completely counterclockwise in BASIC and 127 is completely clockwise). This is just a guess, but it seems simple enough.

Archiving Notes: This is the 300-Baud Bally BASIC version of the program. It has been converted to run in "AstroBASIC" using Jay Fenton's 300 Baud to 2000 Baud Tape Conversion Program (see the "AstroBASIC" user's manual on Pages 104-107). Not one line of code from the 300-Baud version has been changed, which would normally mean that some sound effects no longer work correctly. However, this program doesn't seem to use any sound effects at all.

For additional information , there are more documents available:


http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadian_vol_2/arcadian_vol_02_issue_10.pdf#page=19


Is anyone up for building the interface for this video art program?

Have fun!

15533:
Last week I tried saving some "AstroBASIC" 2000-baud programs to my laptop without success.  I was getting terrible line noise when I was using my Astrocade with my video recording setup.  This is my, probably overly-complicated system:

1) Astrocade, using RF Connection, with RF-out hooked into RF-in of...
2) Blonder Tongue ZDM-306 RF Demodulator with composite-out hooked into composite-in of...
3) Framemeister XRG-Mini Upscaler with HDMI-out hooked into HDMI-in of...
4) AVerMedia Live Gamer Portable with USB-out hooked into USB-in of...
5) Dell Dimension XPS 8700

As you can see, my video recording setup for my Astrocade is rather convoluted!  What's strange, is that I can save from "AstroBASIC" without any issues if I'm using a regular TV, but if I use either of my RF demoluatlors, then the audio-signal out of "AstroBASIC" is so full of line noise that it's actually louder than the expected output signal.

I never noticed this before the end of last week, when on Friday, I realized that I couldn't get a usable signal coming out of the "AstroBASIC" cartridge.  There was terrible noise when I'd record a program.  I got an isolation transformer today and I tried it out.  It not only works, it works better than I could ever have dreamed possible.  This is what I bought:


https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00B2HFE2O/ref=oh_aui_detailpage_o00_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1


The isolation transformer attaches to the end of my Astrocade's RF-out cable.  I like this transformer so much that I actually wrote a review of it for the Amazon page.  Here is my short review, followed by a few more comments:

"Isolation Transformer Works with RF-Out Game Machines and Computers

"I wasn't sure if this would work for me, as my needs are quite specialized.  However, it worked great for my niche computer hobby.

"I'm using a computer game/computer released in January 1978 called the Bally Arcade/Astrocade.  The game system uses RF-out.  I have it hooked up to a demodulator (which converts RF to composite).  The composite output is then hooked up via HDMI (through an X-RGB-Mini Framemeister) to a widescreen LCD monitor.  This RF-output looks fine on the HDMI monitor without the isolation transformer, but just a few days ago I noticed that I could not save any BASIC programs through my system's I/O port: I was getting tons of RF noise within the Astrocade system.  I tried everything that I could think of to fix this problem.  As a last ditch effort, and without much hope, I ordered this 5-2400Mhz isolation transformer.  Maybe it would at least reduce the noise somewhat and allow me to save my programs.  Imagine my surprise that not only did this transformer reduce the noise, it completely removed it.  I mean, literally, if I look at the I/O channel now, there is zero noise present.  All that is there is what is supposed to be there: the computer very clean tape signal.

"I don't understand the technology behind this little miracle device, but whatever it does, it works flawlessly.  My needs are clearly specialized, but if you're working with old game consoles or computers that use RF-out, and you're getting noise in your system's I/O then I would certainly try this $20 device.  I can't believe how good that it works for me!"

I really can't believe how clean the audio signal out of "AstroBASIC" is now that I'm using this isolation transformer.  It went from noisy-as-hell, to absolutely no noise at all.  The audio recordings are completely noise-free: when I amplify a RAW 2000-baud recording using Audacity, it looks nearly-as-good as when I digitally archive an "AstroBASIC" program using Ballybin and AstroWAV.

If you're having any playback/recording issues with either Bally BASIC, then give this a try.  It's a $20 piece of hardware that might just be a miracle-cure for you!

I'm going to try to simplify the technical part if this.Each unit that you are using has it's own ground circuitry. They also have their own oscillators, which injects a bit of noise on each ground system. by the time yo have a ton of items, the noise from these oscillators gets amplified by the amplifiers in each unit. at the end it an be quite a lot. It shows up in the audio because there are circuits that try to eliminate the noise from the video, more that the audio. audio is really susceptible to 60 cycle hum, which is the same frequency as the AC power input. that to can be amplified.The ground loop buster opens up that ground connection between the circuits and sends it on it's own ground circuit.It maybe a 1:1 transformer with a filter to remove any frequency that is audible. That would be called an isolation transformer.

Ken Lill wrote:
>>

Each unit that you are using [to record the Astrocade's output to video] has it's own ground circuitry. [...] The ground loop buster opens up that ground connection between the circuits and sends it on it's own ground circuit.
>>

Thanks for the explanation, Ken.  I followed all kinds of advice to try to reduce the noise in the Astrocade system without getting this transformer, but nothing worked for me.  Frankly, I am rather shocked that the isolation transformer works as well as it does.  It's rather like a magic bullet!

Today, using the isolation transformer, I was able to make video recordings of Jay Fenton's 300-Baud to 2000-Baud conversion utility in-use.  As a test program, I converted the digitally archived 300-baud version of L&M Software's "Air Raid" to 2000-baud.  This program has not been archived in in 2000-baud format.  The conversion program works great, but the "Air Raid" 300-baud format that we have archived is significantly different than the type-in version of "Air Raid" for "AstroBASIC" (which is on BallyAlley.com).  We knew this already, but it's strange to see how significantly different the two BASIC programs are from one another.  It's really neat to see how much faster the Bally BASIC game runs under "AstroBASIC."

Without this isolation transformer, then I would never have been able to record these Baud-rate conversion example videos today (or at all), as the audio-out of the Astrocade was so noisy that audio recordings were basically garbage, just totally unusable.

Adam

Each unit that you are using has it's own ground circuitry. They also have their own oscillators, which injects a bit of noise on each ground system. by the time yo have a ton of items, the noise from these oscillators gets amplified by the amplifiers in each unit. at the end it an be quite a lot. It shows up in the audio because there are circuits that try to eliminate the noise from the video, more that the audio. audio is really susceptible to 60 cycle hum, which is the same frequency as the AC power input. that to can be amplified.
The ground loop buster opens up that ground connection between the circuits and sends it on it's own ground circuit.
It maybe a 1:1 transformer with a filter to remove any frequency that is audible. That would be called an isolation transformer.

Last week I tried saving some "AstroBASIC" 2000-baud programs to my laptop without success.  I was getting terrible line noise when I was using my Astrocade with my video recording setup.  This is my, probably overly-complicated system:

1) Astrocade, using RF Connection, with RF-out hooked into RF-in of...
2) Blonder Tongue ZDM-306 RF Demodulator with composite-out hooked into composite-in of...
3) Framemeister XRG-Mini Upscaler with HDMI-out hooked into HDMI-in of...
4) AVerMedia Live Gamer Portable with USB-out hooked into USB-in of...
5) Dell Dimension XPS 8700

As you can see, my video recording setup for my Astrocade is rather convoluted!  What's strange, is that I can save from "AstroBASIC" without any issues if I'm using a regular TV, but if I use either of my RF demoluatlors, then the audio-signal out of "AstroBASIC" is so full of line noise that it's actually louder than the expected output signal.

I never noticed this before the end of last week, when on Friday, I realized that I couldn't get a usable signal coming out of the "AstroBASIC" cartridge.  There was terrible noise when I'd record a program.  I got an isolation transformer today and I tried it out.  It not only works, it works better than I could ever have dreamed possible.  This is what I bought:

https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00B2HFE2O/ref=oh_aui_detailpage_o00_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1
Amazon.com: Isolation Transformer / Ground Loop Isolator: Electronics<https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00B2HFE2O/ref=oh_aui_detailpage_o00_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1>
www.amazon.com
Amazon.com: Isolation Transformer / Ground Loop Isolator: Electronics


The isolation transformer attaches to the end of my Astrocade's RF-out cable.  I like this transformer so much that I actually wrote a review of it for the Amazon page.  Here is my short review, followed by a few more comments:

"Isolation Transformer Works with RF-Out Game Machines and Computers

"I wasn't sure if this would work for me, as my needs are quite specialized.  However, it worked great for my niche computer hobby.

"I'm using a computer game/computer released in January 1978 called the Bally Arcade/Astrocade.  The game system uses RF-out.  I have it hooked up to a demodulator (which converts RF to composite).  The composite output is then hooked up via HDMI (through an X-RGB-Mini Framemeister) to a widescreen LCD monitor.  This RF-output looks fine on the HDMI monitor without the isolation transformer, but just a few days ago I noticed that I could not save any BASIC programs through my system's I/O port: I was getting tons of RF noise within the Astrocade system.  I tried everything that I could think of to fix this problem.  As a last ditch effort, and without much hope, I ordered this 5-2400Mhz isolation transformer.  Maybe it would at least reduce the noise somewhat and allow me to save my programs.  Imagine my surprise that not only did this transformer reduce the noise, it completely removed it.  I mean, literally, if I look at the I/O channel now, there is zero noise present.  All that is there is what is supposed to be there: the computer very clean tape signal.

"I don't understand the technology behind this little miracle device, but whatever it does, it works flawlessly.  My needs are clearly specialized, but if you're working with old game consoles or computers that use RF-out, and you're getting noise in your system's I/O then I would certainly try this $20 device.  I can't believe how good that it works for me!"

I really can't believe how clean the audio signal out of "AstroBASIC" is now that I'm using this isolation transformer.  It went from noisy-as-hell, to absolutely no noise at all.  The audio recordings are completely noise-free: when I amplify a RAW 2000-baud recording using Audacity, it looks nearly-as-good as when I digitally archive an "AstroBASIC" program using Ballybin and AstroWAV.

If you're having any playback/recording issues with either Bally BASIC, then give this a try.  It's a $20 piece of hardware that might just be a miracle-cure for you!

15539:
I was browsing random issues of "Creative Computing this afternoon when I came across a game that I had never heard of before today: "Bally Artillery" by John W. Rhodes.  This game isn't to be confused with "Artillery Duel" by John Perkins.  Both have the same idea, but they are completely different programs.


Even though this game was published in August 1982, the author seems to imply in his write-up that it was written in late 1978 or early 1979, shortly after he got his Bally Arcade.  This program isn't digitally archived as a WAV file (and likely won't ever be found on tape), so you'll have to type this one into BASIC in order to play it.  You can view the "Bally Artillery" article with the type-in program, here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/type-in_programs/basic/basic.html#BallyArtilleryBASICTypeIn


Here are the authors notes from the "Bally Artillery" article:

"In December of 1978 I was ready to buy my first computer system, but my requirements were not easy to meet. I wanted something that could handle arcade-quality games, had high- resolution graphics capability, color display, and Basic in PROM.

"I was not satisfied with anything my local dealers had to show (no one I visited had a Compucolor. the Apple dealers were showing low-resolution only, and the Atari was only a rumor), but on the basis of the (somewhat premature) advertising for the keyboard/expansion unit. I decided to buy a Bally Professional Arcade. I could use Tiny Basic for a while, and turn it into a “real" machine in just a few short months.

"It was just a few short months later that the local dealers began to show Compucolors and high-resolution Apples, and it seemed that the Bally expansion unit was more of a rumor than the Atari 800. I would visit the showrooms, see those beautiful full-size keyboards, watch people work in “real" Basic and be as green as the color monitors.

"I particularly liked the artillery game that Compucolor called 'Shoot.' This game generates a random terrain display and wind factor and positions two artillery emplacements on the screen so that two opponents can take turns trying to obliterate each other. Eventually I resolved that I either had to buy a Compucolor or program this game on my Bally. I chose the latter.

"This turned out to be quite a challenge with less than 2K of memory and integer-only Tiny Basic. But the Bally Basic is quite sound for game programming and easy to work with. The greatest difficulty was finding an integer sine routine, but after searching the magazines I found a routine to adapt to my purpose. I started out using a full ballistic equation, but soon found by experimentation that I could use an approximation. This eliminated an integer square-root routine and added speed in the bargain.

"I spent approximately two months writing, debugging, and fine-tuning the program, but it was worth the effort.

"A few months later I did buy the Compucolor and have been using it ever since. I'm well satisfied with it and use it for a variety of tasks. But my wife and I still enjoy the Bally for its games, especially the artillery game."


The article also includes notes and an explanation of how the program works.

I'm not sure how I overlooked it before now.  "Bally Artillery" appeared in a major publication.  How has it remained under the radar all of this time?

Enjoy!

Adam

The The Tektronix  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tektronix_4050version of Artillery predated "Artillery duel" by about 7 years? 

 I remember back in college, playing the game on a Tektronix storage scope (A fairly expensive piece of equipment at the time).
 

 Many, many versions of Artillery were out by the time the Bally version showed up.
 

 In fact, I was working on a version myself, but was having problems making the trig routines needed for the game small enough to fit in a cartridge. John had the brilliant idea of creating a 'trig lookup table' of pre-computed values. The table was actually smaller than the room trig routines would take, plus the table was MUCH faster. Which is why he did the Artillery game, and not me. (But I learned that trick from him!)
 

 Brett

I was browsing random issues of "Creative Computing this afternoon when I came across a game that I had never heard of before today: "Bally Artillery" by John W. Rhodes.  This game isn't to be confused with "Artillery Duel" by John Perkins.  Both have the same idea, but they are completely different programs.

Even though this game was published in August 1982, the author seems to imply in his write-up that it was written in late 1978 or early 1979, shortly after he got his Bally Arcade.  This program isn't digitally archived as a WAV file (and likely won't ever be found on tape), so you'll have to type this one into BASIC in order to play it.  You can view the "Bally Artillery" article with the type-in program, here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/type-in_programs/basic/basic.html#BallyArtilleryBASICTypeIn<http://www.ballyalley..com/type-in_programs/basic/basic.html#BallyArtilleryBASICTypeIn>

Here are the authors notes from the "Bally Artillery" article:

"In December of 1978 I was ready to buy my first computer system, but my requirements were not easy to meet. I wanted something that could handle arcade-quality games, had high- resolution graphics capability, color display, and Basic in PROM.

"I was not satisfied with anything my local dealers had to show (no one I visited had a Compucolor. the Apple dealers were showing low-resolution only, and the Atari was only a rumor), but on the basis of the (somewhat premature) advertising for the keyboard/expansion unit. I decided to buy a Bally Professional Arcade. I could use Tiny Basic for a while, and turn it into a “real" machine in just a few short months.

"It was just a few short months later that the local dealers began to show Compucolors and high-resolution Apples, and it seemed that the Bally expansion unit was more of a rumor than the Atari 800. I would visit the showrooms, see those beautiful full-size keyboards, watch people work in “real" Basic and be as green as the color monitors.

"I particularly liked the artillery game that Compucolor called 'Shoot..' This game generates a random terrain display and wind factor and positions two artillery emplacements on the screen so that two opponents can take turns trying to obliterate each other. Eventually I resolved that I either had to buy a Compucolor or program this game on my Bally. I chose the latter.

"This turned out to be quite a challenge with less than 2K of memory and integer-only Tiny Basic. But the Bally Basic is quite sound for game programming and easy to work with. The greatest difficulty was finding an integer sine routine, but after searching the magazines I found a routine to adapt to my purpose. I started out using a full ballistic equation, but soon found by experimentation that I could use an approximation. This eliminated an integer square-root routine and added speed in the bargain.

"I spent approximately two months writing, debugging, and fine-tuning the program, but it was worth the effort.

"A few months later I did buy the Compucolor and have been using it ever since. I'm well satisfied with it and use it for a variety of tasks. But my wife and I still enjoy the Bally for its games, especially the artillery game."

The article also includes notes and an explanation of how the program works.

I'm not sure how I overlooked it before now.  "Bally Artillery" appeared in a major publication.  How has it remained under the radar all of this time?

Enjoy!

Adam

The original Bally Arcade/Astrocade BASIC version of John Perkins' Artillery Duel (first published in the May 19, 1980 issue of the Arcadian newsletter on pages 58 ...

The BASIC version of Artillery Duel, first published in the May 1980 Arcadian, is quite good.  It also is faster than I would normally expect out of BASIC.  Xonox released Artillery Duel on cartridge on many of the 8-bit home computers and game consoles.  I've read that John Perkins programmed some of them (I think the Atari 2600 and maybe the Colecovision versions?).  The Astrocade's Artillery Duel is the best version of the game (for 8-bit systems)-- I just wish that you didn't have to watch the marching soldiers every time you play the game.


I tried to find a video of someone playing an artillery game on a Tektronix scope, but I had no luck locating one.  I did find videos of people playing much more sophisticated games like Quake (!) and consoles systems like Sega and Nintendo being displayed on oscilloscopes.  Very strange-- but cool!  I sure miss vector games like Tempest, Omega Race and Asteroids.

Adam

The The Tektronix <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tektronix_4050> version of Artillery predated "Artillery duel" by about 7 years?

I remember back in college, playing the game on a Tektronix storage scope (A fairly expensive piece of equipment at the time).

Many, many versions of Artillery were out by the time the Bally version showed up.

In fact, I was working on a version myself, but was having problems making the trig routines needed for the game small enough to fit in a cartridge. John had the brilliant idea of creating a 'trig lookup table' of pre-computed values. The table was actually smaller than the room trig routines would take, plus the table was MUCH faster. Which is why he did the Artillery game, and not me. (But I learned that trick from him!)

 I was browsing random issues of "Creative Computing this afternoon when I came across a game that I had never heard of before today: "Bally Artillery" by John W. Rhodes.  This game isn't to be confused with "Artillery Duel" by John Perkins.  Both have the same idea, but they are completely different programs.
Even though this game was published in August 1982, the author seems to imply in his write-up that it was written in late 1978 or early 1979, shortly after he got his Bally Arcade.  This program isn't digitally archived as a WAV file (and likely won't ever be found on tape), so you'll have to type this one into BASIC in order to play it.  You can view the "Bally Artillery" article with the type-in program, here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/type-in_programs/basic/basic.html#BallyArtilleryBASICTypeIn
Here are the authors notes from the "Bally Artillery" article:

"In December of 1978 I was ready to buy my first computer system, but my requirements were not easy to meet. I wanted something that could handle arcade-quality games, had high- resolution graphics capability, color display, and Basic in PROM.

"I was not satisfied with anything my local dealers had to show (no one I visited had a Compucolor. the Apple dealers were showing low-resolution only, and the Atari was only a rumor), but on the basis of the (somewhat premature) advertising for the keyboard/expansion unit. I decided to buy a Bally Professional Arcade. I could use Tiny Basic for a while, and turn it into a “real" machine in just a few short months.

"It was just a few short months later that the local dealers began to show Compucolors and high-resolution Apples, and it seemed that the Bally expansion unit was more of a rumor than the Atari 800. I would visit the showrooms, see those beautiful full-size keyboards, watch people work in “real" Basic and be as green as the color monitors.

"I particularly liked the artillery game that Compucolor called 'Shoot...' This game generates a random terrain display and wind factor and positions two artillery emplacements on the screen so that two opponents can take turns trying to obliterate each other. Eventually I resolved that I either had to buy a Compucolor or program this game on my Bally. I chose the latter.

"This turned out to be quite a challenge with less than 2K of memory and integer-only Tiny Basic. But the Bally Basic is quite sound for game programming and easy to work with. The greatest difficulty was finding an integer sine routine, but after searching the magazines I found a routine to adapt to my purpose. I started out using a full ballistic equation, but soon found by experimentation that I could use an approximation. This eliminated an integer square-root routine and added speed in the bargain.

"I spent approximately two months writing, debugging, and fine-tuning the program, but it was worth the effort.

"A few months later I did buy the Compucolor and have been using it ever since. I'm well satisfied with it and use it for a variety of tasks. But my wife and I still enjoy the Bally for its games, especially the artillery game."

The article also includes notes and an explanation of how the program works.

I'm not sure how I overlooked it before now.  "Bally Artillery" appeared in a major publication.  How has it remained under the radar all of this time?

Enjoy!

Adam

I don’t know that much about programming, but all you need trig for is to convert the angle+strength into X+Y starting velocity.  Wind effects X, gravity effects Y and is a constant 9.8.   Once it’s in XY, it’s just combining.
It doesn’t need to be in terms of m/s/s  Gravity can be in Gs where gravity is 1 and so many bags equal so many g.  You would express wind in G x seconds for non-decimal computing.

Maybe the game uses some simple version of sound effects derived from this old-style (circa 1978/1979) method of creating sound effects.  This would make sense if the game really was written, as the author seems to imply, in 1978 or or 1979. Ken Lill wrote:
>>
Any game is hackable. However, it would take some one like Michael Garber or Richard Degler to find the board layout area.
>>

Sure, that's true; any game is hackable, but some games are easier to hack than others.  By asking if BallyPin is "hackable," I was wondering if BallyBin can just have its graphics rearranged, which would allow new levels to be created easily.  I highly doubt that this is the case, but I suppose it's possible.

>>
it would take a GOOD programmer to do all of the research and make a "do" file of all of the different factors involves. If we had the original source code, THAT would help.
>>

Yes, having the original source code for Ballybin would be helpful, but I think that's long gone; it's simply been lost to the ages.

For those that are curious, we don't need a Bally Pin cartridge to hack the game.  The cartridges contents were dumped in the 1990s.  If the cartridge does get hacked, then the hacked contents would then be placed on an EPROM and used on real hardware (or simply as a ROM image under MAME).  It's even easier to hack the game and just try it out in the Astrocade emulator in MAME.

Just for fun, I opened the 4K BallyPin.bin ROM image in a hex editor (HxD) and "printed" the ROM contents as a pdf file (I padded the beginning of the file to make the hex addresses start at $2000, the beginning of the cartridge area in the Astrocade's memory map).

If you look at the hex contents in this pdf, then you'll notice that the first byte is $55 (with is referred to by Bally's 8K ROM as the system sentinel byte).  Knowing that first byte is $55 is very helpful.  From there, you can begin hacking the file rather "easily," because a $55 means that the cartridge is a standard Bally Arcade ROM that uses the system menu and therefore follows standard conventions that are laid out in the "Nutting Manual."

The $55 isn't some random byte.  It's a "U" in ASCII because the user menu is going to be used to start the game.  The next bytes all deal with interacting with the ROMs user menu.  The third set of two bytes tells where the game starts in ROM, which is at $2107.  Then it's a "simple" matter of using the Z80 disassembler DZ80 with the DZ80 Dissassembler Script (which "understands" calls to the System ROM) to start figuring out the code.  Point DZ80 at $2107 and let it go until the end of the file and see what you get.

Getting the hex bytes into z80 source code isn't too hard; it's mostly just time consuming.  You have to follow the code a little at a time to make sure that you don't accidentally start disassembling areas of the ROM which are actually data.  Once the source code is available, then a user can begin to follow the code to understand what it is doing.  That's the part that is time consuming.  However, what I've described so far, in my eyes, is simple hacking.  With this much done, the graphics can be found, changed and then you can see what effects this has on the Bally Pin's pinball tables.

For those of you who have no idea what I'm talking about in this post, then here's a fun tidbit.  If you look toward the end of the ROM file in the attached pdf, then you'll also notice the phrases "BALLY PIN 1" and "BALLY PIN 2" appear in ASCII.  This is used by the user menu.  Change those few letters and anything you want will appear in the menu.  This is how the Astrocade game called Pac-Man was changed to Muncher when it was released in the 1980s.  Both words have seven letters, so it was an easy "hack."

Adam

I added a preliminary Z80 disassembly of Bally Pin (aka Astrocade Pinball) to BallyAlley.com.  This game was released in 1979 by Bally Mfg. Corp.  It was programmed by Bob Ogdon and the audio was created by Scot Norris.

The idea to hack the tables in Bally Pin led to this disassembly of the game. Only about 2 1/2 hours were spent on this disassembly. It's really just an example of how quickly progress can be made using some of the tools available on BallyAlley.com.

Here is a link to the Bally Pin disassembly:


http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/ml_source.html#BallyPinDisassembly

If, for some reason, this link doesn't work, then here is a link to only the source page:


http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/ml_source.html


The tools used to disassemble the Bally Pin binary image to Z80 source code are:

1) Z80 2.0 - A Z80 Disassembler
2) DZ80 Dissassembler Script - Required to disassemble Astrocade ROM routines.
3) HVGLIB.H - Home Video Game Library Equates.

These disassembly tools are available here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_tools/ml_tools.html


This source code assembles to a byte-for-byte identical ROM image of Bally Pin using the Zmac cross-assembler.

These are many, MANY more areas of the code that are called or jumped-to in the already disassembled part of the game. Without much effort, I suppose much of this game can be disassembled.  The trick is following the code and understanding what is going on that is time consuming.  From my brief look at the code so far, it seems that the tables are drawn with rectangles.

If anyone decides to continue to disassemble this code, then please let me know.  I'd like to put any additional efforts online at BallyAlley.com.

I have a hope that this short peek at the game's code will inspire someone to dig into the code and make a hack to add new tables for the game.

Have fun!

Adam

I remember back in college, playing the game on a Tektronix storage scope (A fairly expensive piece of equipment at the time).
Many, many versions of Artillery were out by the time the Bally version showed up.
In fact, I was working on a version myself, but was having problems making the trig routines needed for the game small enough to fit in a cartridge. John had the brilliant idea of creating a 'trig lookup table' of pre-computed values. The table was actually smaller than the room trig routines would take, plus the table was MUCH faster. Which is why he did the Artillery game, and not me. (But I learned that trick from him!)
Brett

I designed the ICBM controller, and I don't even have one (so, yes they are rare). 

 But I do believe that both Michael Toth and Marion Nalepa (my partners at Spectre Systems), have ICBM controllers. They 'might' be persuaded to part with them for the right price...
 

 I really would like to build a few more, but I just don't have the time.

Based on what I know, which is VERY little, one Astrocade paddle maps to one axis, the other paddle maps to the other axis, (I don’t know whether it’s a square or circle restrictor, but hat would mater)  The 5200 has no centering resistance, which I believe it makes it more ideal for a Missile Command-type game (which I assume ICBM is,)  than one with a centering resistance.(but I don’t know what the original controller had).

And I assume each cardinal and the 2 fire buttons represent one of each of the 1 buttons, and can be all pressed independently.

I suggested on the AtariAge website, for a Jaguar party game collection I call "Going Jag", (a la Mario Party, Sonic Shuffle, Pac Man Fever, or Crash Bash), a "finger bomb mini game" where you have to press 4-6 buttons on the keypad, and lift one finger, and press it elsewhere.   (you might have to press one button with two fingers to free another finger.  In theory the Astrocade ICBM controller should work on the same principle.  So one could program a 2-player (4 ports=2 players) race to diffuse the bomb.   But one wrong step, you set off the bomb.   Some feel free to program that.  I don’t lknwo if I can run it fast enough to be an action game, but maybe a prototype can function on Bally Basic.  Maybe a multi-load party game, called "Kiss My Astrocade" can be made.

OK, I went and looked at some old notes... 

 Here is how things map...
 

 Joystick left/right = Player 1 knob
 Joystick up/down = Player 2 knob
 

 Left missile base     = Player 1 joystick left
 Center missile base = Player 1 trigger
 Right missile base   = Player 1 joystick right
 

 Start game = Player 2 trigger
 

 This is all that needs to be wired up to make a ICBM Attack game controller.
 

 Getting the 9-pin D-connector cables might be a little tricky. I don't know where to get them anymore.
 And finding a workable X-Y Joystick these days would be hard too. (The resistance just needs to be the same as the Bally handle knob value.)
 

 Also, 4 pinball buttons (3 for the bases, 1 to start the game)
 And a case.
 

 A pretty simple project. Again, doing it is just a matter of time. :-(
 

 Brett

15595:
Assuming ICBM Attack is a Missile Command-type game, it makes more sense to be no-resistance.   A lot of the 5200 games make more sense (at least the ones that use the analog stick in an analog way, not the ones that are better as digital) with a non centering joystick.   Typical paddle games make more sense with a non-centering control.

Don’t believe me? Try playing an Atari 2600 paddle game in "absolute mode" on an Xbox One thumbpad.  (absolute mode more accurately emulates a 2600 paddle better than relative mode.)  It takes a LOT MORE energy and focus to "dial a position" on a thumbstick that has centering resistance than dialing a position on a real 2600 paddle or 5200 joystick..   I would rate the Atari Flashback series on 56ok.org <http://56ok.org/> a bad rating for that physical problem combined with high ping, but I never found an opponent/partner to play a 2600 game online, so I can’t give a definitive rating, because 56ok’s main purpose is about gaming at lower than recommended bandwidths. (And not by choice.  There’s no faster internet where I live.)

> I suggested on the AtariAge website, for a Jaguar party game collection I call "Going Jag", (a la Mario Party, Sonic Shuffle, Pac Man Fever, or Crash Bash), a "finger bomb mini game" where you have to press 4-6 buttons on the keypad, and lift one finger, and press it elsewhere.   (you might have to press one button with two fingers to free another finger.  In theory the Astrocade ICBM controller should work on the same principle.  So one could program a 2-player (4 ports=2 players) race to diffuse the bomb.   But one wrong step, you set off the bomb.   Some feel free to program that.  I don’t lknwo if I can run it fast enough to be an action game, but maybe a prototype can function on Bally Basic.  Maybe a multi-load party game, called "Kiss My Astrocade" can be made.

Well, looking at the schematics, and knowing what I know about Bally Basic,  Each direction is NOT independent in terms of computer logic.   Meaning the Astrocade understands a trinary value of a directional axis either pressed one way, pressed the other way, or pressed neither way.   I looks like with the extra buttons, if multiple keypad buttons are pressed, it may have the possibility of having "both north and south" as a possible value.  But the only acceptable values on an axis are -1, 0, and +1.  What would happen if you pressed 2 keys that mapped to the same controller axis in opposite direcitons.  What would the value of JX(0) be if left and right wee simultaneously pushed, like on the ICBM controller?  That shots don’t my idea of Finger Twisted Bomb.   But on the AtariAge.com <http://atariage.com/> Jaguar, people say the keypad has 12 independent buttons, instead of 12 buttons dependent on the fact only one button gets pressed at a time.

Whoever invented and used the Hitbox had an unfair advantage in Street Fighter games by being able to simultaneously press forward and back, or blocking and going forward. The only way Hitboxes are legal nowadays is if you add a Simultaneous Opposite Cardinal Direction Scrubber, or SOCD Scrubber to the controller.  It’s an added something that prevents the left+right move.  Now software deals with the SOCD issue, but the Genesis or SNES version didn’t have to deal with that because joysticks were designed to physically disable east+west through a physical mechanism which wouldn’t be both be touched simultaneously, which is basically, the joystick itself.  There were strange effects when doing that, some of which would be considered unnatural. Crossups would not work.

If anyone has a Hitbox that’s connectable to a Sega Genesis, Master System, Atari 7800, Colecovision, or Atari 2600, make (I would like to buy one, but no one would want to be hired to build one, Those who can, do.  Those who can’t, hire, not teach.) an Atari Joystick-to-Bally Console adapter for just the joystick, (I understand, for the cheap version, only the joystick would work, and not the paddle.   I know that perfectly well.  And frankly, any game using the paddle or both the paddle and stick I’d rather play with a real Bally controller, of which I have 4), take out (if it’s temporary) or deactivate (if it’s permanent) the SOCD scrubber, and see what happens f you press North + South, or East + West.

Can’t take out the SOCD scrubber easily? Try an Atari 2600 Track And Field Controller. It has an independent left and right as the 2 run buttons.  You get faster times becuase there are times when you press Left and right together, and will not be ignored.

The website where schematics to both and Atari->Bally, and a Bally-> Atari controller adapter are here: http://www.glankonian.com/~lance/Hack.html <http://www.glankonian.com/~lance/Hack.html>  It looks like a simple pin swap, no complex electronic engineering needed (unless you want to deal with the paddles.) except for wiring one pin input to a different pin output.  A DB9 M to F would work

I tried a Track N Field controller on Space Invaders for the 2600, you either stand still or slightly flicker left and right.  My guess is the first, where it moves you one unit to the left then one to the right before the next frame is drawn, yet happens so fast it looks like standing still.  I remembered the net result, which is that I didn’t move.

The fact that the Astrocade marries the 2 poles and makes it trinary makes me wonder what the result of E+W or N+S is.  Anyone know what the result of pressing N+S or E+W is?  And Yes, I know you can’t do that physically with a real Astrocade joystick without seriously ruining it.  It’s obviously too late to add a JX(P)=2 for E(P)+W(P) for the ICBM controller, that would requiring making a new Bally Basic cart (let alone the other higher programable Bally programs.),and, trust me, NO ONE is going to make a new Bally Basic Cart just to accommodate 10 independent buttons on the ICBM keypad, just for my crazy idea of Finger Twister Bomb.

No, I’m talking about the border of the xy.   Is it circular shape, meaning the maximum radius equals the maximum value of x or y, meaning it’s physically impossible to go 100 % + 100% e because that’s 141% NE?  IS it square shaped where 100% N + 100% E is achievable?

If it’s an XY basis, then the restrictor is square, meaning  it’s so many x and so many y.   However most analog controllers nowadays have circular restrictors.  meaning the maximum radius is 1, or the maximum X individually or the maximum Y individually.  Electronically, you could have maximum X and Maximum Y, but if it were recognized in terms of angle and length, the angle would be 45 degrees, but, even though electronically the length can equal 1.41, the circular restrictor makes the maximum length 1 by force of physics.

On a tangentially related note: That is an issue I have in using a digital joystick to actuate an analog joypad.  For Metal Slug Anthology for the Wii, I don’t know if I’ll get errors when my fight stick equals an analog stick press.  Either the joystick and digital-to-analog converter must be fixed to have a maximum length of 1 when pressing diagonals, yet 1 also in the cardinals,   I don’t know about that.

Similarly there is a digital joystick for the Atari 5200 which is called the Comeptition Pro Joystick, which is an aracde style joystick which, when used on Missile Command (a game designed to be analog), jumps immediatety from center when centered to the top of the screen when pressed up, and to the top right corner when pressed NE.  There are only 9 contact points. 15626:
You missed my point:  Is it square, like an Aple IIe controller, or is it circular, like a modern Analog controller.

I understand they were originally designed as 2 separate 1-dimenisonal knobs for 2 separate players, and that’s how Bally Basic and higher Bally languages see the ICBM controller.

It’s important whether the 2-dimension ICBM stick is square or circular.   Rectangular allows maximum independent range of X and Y, or KN(0) and KN(1).

A circular hole restricts the vlaues so if x and y are percentages of maxiimum unidirectional actuation, (from center to edge, not edge to edge) then x^2 + Y^2 <= 100%^2 where 100 is the maximum center to edge value of one knob independently (for the purposes of this exercise, NOT for the purposes of Bally Basic or higher Bally programming languages).    if the game was originally designed for a rectangular controller, and you use a circular one, all the points on the corners are unreachable outside the X^2+Y^2=100%^2 circle.  If the upper right corner X=+100% and y=+100%, and that in theory should be reachable according to the code, then in practice, the extreme Northeast corner is unreachable becuase 100% ^ 2+ 100% ^2 = r^2 =200% r=141% and if the restrictor is physically a circle, then, even if the code thinks that +100,+100 is reachable, and there’s no errors in code, then the joystick itself limits you by keeping a radius of 100%.  The software dowesn’t know the difference, but in order for you to reach (+100,+100) you have to break your circular restrictor to reach (+100,+100)

It’s basic high school (maybe earlier if you were in advanced classes) trigonometry. A circular restrictor, assuming it’s not broken, is designed so that it’s a lazy system designer's way of enforcing the rule against "diagonal speed boosts" in an analog environment.  read http://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DiagonalSpeedBoost <http://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DiagonalSpeedBoost> for how this affects movement in some games, and ways to combat that.

A system has to take into account its standards.  Apple IIe is designed with a rectangular restrictor.   Therefore, the language in the program has to restrict the diagonal speed boost on it's own (if that is the desired effect)   The posiitve is that if the joystick represents a TV screen, every point on the TV screen can be reached in an instant if you use absolute positional X/Y analog controls.

If you use an N64, or any other controller more modern.  It’s circular.   The good news is that the maximum speeed is physically enforced by the limiter, as opposed to code.   The downside is if you use the circle to represent the absolute position on an X/Y screen, every conceivable diagonal beyond the range of one axis alone is untouchable.

I assume that the ICBM game is Bally’s version of Missile Command.  If that is right, I can draw a stationary picture showing the folly of a circular restrictor if the original makers decided on a square restrictor. Give me an hour and I can either computer draw, or find an existing diagram showing what I mean

On the 5200 version of Missile Command, even though the joystick, if I remember right, is circular, it’s programmed to be reachable on every pixel of the screen by having an outer dead zone border.   If the ICBM controller is designed to be square, and you replace it with a circle, then the corners would be unreachable.    However, if code in the game suggests a corner dead-zone where basically it only takes into account the square that can fit within the circle, it doesn’t matter what you use.  Look for an number that equals about 70% of the center-to-edge length of one axis.   If that is there, it’s be funny moving more precisely away from a corner or edge, but is doable.   If there is no 70% in the appropriate code, then the joystick was designed to be in a square restrictor.

Just by the fact that all TV screens are RECTANGULAR makes a square not reach the corners in the X direction OR goes way beyond in the Y direction, But in either case, the proper adjusting of the parallel resistor's size can over come any dead spots, rectangular OR round. Using an 8 direction like most digital controllers, gives a lot of space that is unreachable. If its square then they will have to be a different set fo values. So ANY controller can be adjusted to work. I  am also confident that the designers of the game knew the limitations of the controllers being used and didn't start out with the missiles coming from the extreme corners. It’s important whether the 2-dimension ICBM stick is square or circular.   Rectangular allows maximum independent range of X and Y, or KN(0) and KN(1).
A circular hole restricts the vlaues so if x and y are percentages of maxiimum unidirectional actuation, (from center to edge, not edge to edge) then x^2 + Y^2 <= 100%^2 where 100 is the maximum center to edge value of one knob independently (for the purposes of this exercise, NOT for the purposes of Bally Basic or higher Bally programming languages).    if the game was originally designed for a rectangular controller, and you use a circular one, all the points on the corners are unreachable outside the X^2+Y^2=100%^2 circle.  If the upper right corner X=+100% and y=+100%, and that in theory should be reachable according to the code, then in practice, the extreme Northeast corner is unreachable becuase 100% ^ 2+ 100% ^2 = r^2 =200% r=141% and if the restrictor is physically a circle, then, even if the code thinks that +100,+100 is reachable, and there’s no errors in code, then the joystick itself limits you by keeping a radius of 100%.  The software dowesn’t know the difference, but in order for you to reach (+100,+100) you have to break your circular restrictor to reach (+100,+100)
It’s basic high school (maybe earlier if you were in advanced classes) trigonometry. A system has to take into account its standards.  Apple IIe is designed with a rectangular restrictor.   Therefore, the language in the program has to restrict the diagonal speed boost on it's own (if that is the desired effect)   The posiitve is that if the joystick represents a TV screen, every point on the TV screen can be reached in an instant if you use absolute positional X/Y analog controls.
If you use an N64, or any other controller more modern.  It’s circular.   The good news is that the maximum speeed is physically enforced by the limiter, as opposed to code.   The downside is if you use the circle to represent the absolute position on an X/Y screen, every conceivable diagonal beyond the range of one axis alone is untouchable.
I assume that the ICBM game is Bally’s version of Missile Command.  If that is right, I can draw a stationary picture showing the folly of a circular restrictor if the original makers decided on a square restrictor. Give me an hour and I can either computer draw, or find an existing diagram showing what I mean
On the 5200 version of Missile Command, even though the joystick, if I remember right, is circular, it’s programmed to be reachable on every pixel of the screen by having an outer dead zone border.   If the ICBM controller is designed to be square, and you replace it with a circle, then the corners would be unreachable.    However, if code in the game suggests a corner dead-zone where basically it only takes into account the square that can fit within the circle, it doesn’t matter what you use.  Look for an number that equals about 70% of the center-to-edge length of one axis.   If that is there, it’s be funny moving more precisely away from a corner or edge, but is doable.   If there is no 70% in the appropriate code, then the joystick was designed to be in a square restrictor.

Hi, everyone.  It's nice to hear people talking about the ICBM Attack controller, especially since I've been disasembling Bally Pin.  Bally Pin can take advantage of that special controller's side-buttons, which were made especially for that pinball game.


I've played ICBM Attack in MAME and it works great.  This game is based on the idea of Missile Command, but it's not that game.  It's different from it enough that it stands on its own.


I've used many different analog controllers (various mice, trackballs, X-box 360, and PS2-like controllers) to play ICBM Attack in MAME.  They all work fine without restricted movements.  The X-Arcade trackball works flawlessly; it's as though the game was designed for that from-the-future controller.  Using self-centering controllers doesn't work well at all, as the cursor keeps moving back to the middle of the screen (which is what you would expect with such a controller).  Since most people don't have trackballs, then use the mouse it works better than you might expect with this game.


Give ICBM Attack a try in MAME.  I wrote instructions with Paul Thacker on how to do that in 2010.  You can read them here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/ballyalley/articles/Playing_ICBM_Attack_Using_MESS.pdf


The instructions are a little outdated, but if you're familiar with MAME, then you won't have any issues setting the emulator up to play this game with an analog controller.


Above all else, please try ICBM Attack under emulation.  It's a great game that no one has played properly on their real Astrocade systems, probably, since the 1980s or 1990s.  What's cool about this game having been placed into the public domain is that anyone can try it out under Astrocade emulation.  I've said it many times, but I'm going to say it again: thanks to Brett and the gang at Spectre for allowing people to share and try ICBM Attack going on 35 years after it was written.  It's a rare game in cartridge form, but it's common in the virtual world.  Unlike most rare games for consoles, this rare game isn't terrible: it's damn good!


Enjoy the game, and have fun using your Astrocade, be it made of plastic and silicon from the 1970s and 1980s, or an "Astrocade" that you're using on your modern system via the MAME emulator.


One last thing, how good does MAME work on the Mac?


Adam

You missed my point:  Is it square, like an Aple IIe controller, or is it circular, like a modern Analog controller.

I understand they were originally designed as 2 separate 1-dimenisonal knobs for 2 separate players, and that’s how Bally Basic and higher Bally languages see the ICBM controller.

It’s important whether the 2-dimension ICBM stick is square or circular.   Rectangular allows maximum independent range of X and Y, or KN(0) and KN(1).

A circular hole restricts the vlaues so if x and y are percentages of maxiimum unidirectional actuation, (from center to edge, not edge to edge) then x^2 + Y^2 <= 100%^2 where 100 is the maximum center to edge value of one knob independently (for the purposes of this exercise, NOT for the purposes of Bally Basic or higher Bally programming languages).    if the game was originally designed for a rectangular controller, and you use a circular one, all the points on the corners are unreachable outside the X^2+Y^2=100%^2 circle.  If the upper right corner X=+100% and y=+100%, and that in theory should be reachable according to the code, then in practice, the extreme Northeast corner is unreachable becuase 100% ^ 2+ 100% ^2 = r^2 =200% r=141% and if the restrictor is physically a circle, then, even if the code thinks that +100,+100 is reachable, and there’s no errors in code, then the joystick itself limits you by keeping a radius of 100%.  The software dowesn’t know the difference, but in order for you to reach (+100,+100) you have to break your circular restrictor to reach (+100,+100)

It’s basic high school (maybe earlier if you were in advanced classes) trigonometry. A circular restrictor, assuming it’s not broken, is designed so that it’s a lazy system designer's way of enforcing the rule against "diagonal speed boosts" in an analog environment.  read http://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DiagonalSpeedBoost for how this affects movement in some games, and ways to combat that.
[http://static.tvtropes.org/logo_blue_small.png]<http://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DiagonalSpeedBoost>

Diagonal Speed Boost - TV Tropes<http://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DiagonalSpeedBoost>
tvtropes.org
The Diagonal Speed Boost trope as used in popular culture. You're headed north, he's headed northeast, he suddenly turns northwest halfway to the destination …


A system has to take into account its standards.  Apple IIe is designed with a rectangular restrictor.   Therefore, the language in the program has to restrict the diagonal speed boost on it's own (if that is the desired effect)   The posiitve is that if the joystick represents a TV screen, every point on the TV screen can be reached in an instant if you use absolute positional X/Y analog controls.

If you use an N64, or any other controller more modern.  It’s circular.   The good news is that the maximum speeed is physically enforced by the limiter, as opposed to code.   The downside is if you use the circle to represent the absolute position on an X/Y screen, every conceivable diagonal beyond the range of one axis alone is untouchable.

I assume that the ICBM game is Bally’s version of Missile Command.  If that is right, I can draw a stationary picture showing the folly of a circular restrictor if the original makers decided on a square restrictor. Give me an hour and I can either computer draw, or find an existing diagram showing what I mean

On the 5200 version of Missile Command, even though the joystick, if I remember right, is circular, it’s programmed to be reachable on every pixel of the screen by having an outer dead zone border.   If the ICBM controller is designed to be square, and you replace it with a circle, then the corners would be unreachable.    However, if code in the game suggests a corner dead-zone where basically it only takes into account the square that can fit within the circle, it doesn’t matter what you use.  Look for an number that equals about 70% of the center-to-edge length of one axis.   If that is there, it’s be funny moving more precisely away from a corner or edge, but is doable.   If there is no 70% in the appropriate code, then the joystick was designed to be in a square restrictor.

Using a real Astrocade for most people is pretty difficult.  Even though I have a few working real Astrocades, I still find that using an Astrocade emulator is very helpful.  Probably the most useful reason is for MAME's debugger, which gives a programmer (or casual-at-best programmer, like me) many ways to follow a program's logic.  Need to know what's in HL, A, or IX, then just stop the program when it reach a certain part of the code and see what's in memory.  Wanna go through a program line by line.  No problem.  Want to run a program for a few iterations and then see what happens at a certain point.  It can be done.  MAME is great for programmers, but since Astrocade's are hard to come by, it's great for casual users too.


Adam

15649:
I don't know if I'll have more MAME debugger examples, but I've called this thread #1.  Who knows if there will be more of them.

Today while disassembling Bally Pin, I found the table that holds the six "scores" (sound effects) that are called by BMUSIC.  Here is the source code for that that I created.  Note that L stand for Label here, so L2F7A means that a score is at $2F7A on the cartridge.


; Music Score Table ??
L2F6E:  DW      L2F7A
        DW      L2FE6
        DW      L2FA3
        DW      L2FB8
        DW      L2FC2
        DW      L2FCA

Each score is called by the BMUSIC routine, which resides at ROM location $2F67 on the Bally Pin cartridge.  I set a MAME debugger breakpoint at $2F67.  This allowed me to check what was going on with various registers when BMUSIC is called.  I needed to know the values of HL, A and IX.  This worked okay, but was a little clumsy.  I wondered how to set a breakpoint only when HL was a certain value.  I looked online, but I couldn't find exactly what I was looking for exactly.

Through trial and error, I discovered that I could stop Bally Pin's execution when the BMUSIC routine was called and one certain score was called.  Here's how I did this in MAME's debugger:

BPSET $2F67,HL == $2FC2

This allowed me to figure-out that the "score" at $2FC2 is the one of the two sounds that the spinner makes as it goes round and round.

MAME's debugger is sweet!  It's too bad that the documentation for it is sparse.  You sort of need to know how to use it before you start using it, which is intimidating.

I honestly never seen an ICBM controller, so I don’t know if it orginally had a square restrictor or a circular restrictor.   If the original was circular then the code compensates for that.  But if the original had a square restrictor, and the neo-ICBM controllers use PC analog controllers with Circular Restrictors, then you’ll get problems of not being able to reach the corners.

I’m not an expert i game coding.   I’m just bringing up one problem I see that others are too busy looking at other stuff to see.

If you’re going to retrofit a controller, then make sure it has a square restrictor like the Apple IIe controller.

By the way, I googled the difference between a circular and square restrictor in analog joysticks, all I could find are articles of fighting game sticks, which are digital.

I suspect my issue is related to why a few digital games dont work well with a Competition Pro Joystick for the 5200.  it scrapes the potentiometer at extreme X and Y values at the 4 directions, and combines one X scrape and one Y scrape for each diagonal, and has a default scrape in the center of an axis when nothing else in  that axis is activated..  There are a couple of 5200 games, Popeye and Mountain King, where it sounds like it should be playable with a digital joystick, but it isn’t.   I guess they are both 4 way games, that look to see if any analog angle is closer to the vertical or horizontal axis, and may also assume the if X > +/- .707 then y by definition of a circular restrictor is automatically less than .707 so it doesn’t do a check in the code, not anticipating a situation where x=1 and y=1, if the Competition pro just scrapes the potentiometer at extreme points along each axis, and when the assumption of the physical circular restrictor is no longer in play, the code does something unexpected when you do a diagonal.

How come no one is acknowledging my issue?   Better me see the potential problem now, than the ICBM Joystick maker finding about it later after a prototype is built, but can’t mysteriously reach the extreme corners.   Then you have to start over, and that wastes money.   And if I save you guys a PC joystick prototype by considering the restrictor, than all I ask for is a thanks on the official credits of the product’s website.   No money.
