15657:
Thank you for showing me the link.   I guess I was worried about something which wasn’t an issue.

I just remember my Apple IIe had a square restrictor, and the 5200 Competiiotn Pro treats the twin X/Y analogs as if it were in a a square restrictor in terms of values X or y can only equal one of these 3 values: -1.00, 0.00, or +1.00 Nothing in between, but the original Atari controller had a circular restrictor, which
even though the potentiometers can reach -1, 0, and 0, the physical restrictor prevents any simultaneous combination of X=+/- 1 and Y=+/-1.

But since Spectre the company that both programmed the game and built the prototype joystick intended it with a circular restrictor, then maintaining a circular restrictor makes the hand fit in the glove perfectly.   In fact if it were a square restrictor in the new version, depending on the programming can lead to either just a dead zone buffer on the 4 sides to programming errors if the joystick was extended into the restricted zone of a circular restrictor that is reachable in a square restrictor environment.

Better me bring it up and we come to a resolution than no one bring it up and have it turn out to be in error.  Saves time, saves money.

Now the other issue.  No-resistance analog movement.  I know this is an issue because if you’ve ever played an Atari analog game on the Xbox One, which doesn’t let you plug in paddles, and if you want to physically recreate the instant "dial a position" of an original Atari paddle, it’s a lot harder if you have to fight centering resistance found in a typical analog stick today. You controls would be uncomfortably tough.  Many people who never used an Atari 2600 paddle don’t know the precision and quickness of dialing a position on a CRT TV.   If I didn’t know better, I’d say Breakout and Warlords suck with such a control scheme.  And the fact the don’t let you attach paddles is shortsighted of Atari.

Of course that requires the selling of Xbox One paddles, or at least an Atari 9-pin to Xbox/PS4 USB adapter.  (the PS4 has a better solution of using the track-pad to instantly dial a position.  I don’t know how well that works on a PS4, but it’s probably more acceptable than fighting the centering resistance of the default analog pad.) The reason why new Xbox One and PS4 paddles aren’t released are because, outside of these games, there would be no use for one dimensional potentiometers with no centering resistance.   Most games rely on the fact that the standard controller auto centers.

The Atari Flashback games weren’t exactly blockbusters, based on the online traffic of those games, so there’d be no point in releasing it.  Anyone who actually really cares about that stuff probably has a real 2600 and a real CRT TV.  Probably prohibitive licensing of Microsoft and Sony prevents the paddle adapters to be made in a low-cost manner.  Half the reason why I bought those games were playing these multiplayer games online.  I was going to test it for 56ok.org <http://56ok.org/> but I LITERALLY found no one willing to play on DAY ONE when it first came out, let alone play the games I wanted to play.  But the controls and a lack of a CRT mess it up enough anyway that the ONLY joy would be found in online play, but all I get are crickets.

I heard the easiest solution is taking out the spring, and hope the Astrocade doesn’t base its centering off an initial position, like N64 controllers and later.   If they are like Artari Paddles and 5200 controllers, that should be good.

By the way, can you use buttons 1, 2, and 3 as the 3 bases, and the S as start.   If you need 3 pinball buttons, then what do you need pinball buttons for ICBM Attack, unless it was going to be advertised with the phrase "Use on Bally Pinball with real pinball buttons".

By the way, if I understand the Bally Asrocade system right, you can’t make a 10 button game where any combination of buttons is pressed, becuase JX(p) and J(Y(p) can only equal 3 values, pressed one way, pressed the other, or neutral.  What happens if the JX(0)=1 button is pressed at the same time as the JX(0)=-1 is pressed when they are on 2 different physical buttons..  The Astrocade wouldn’t know what to do.   It’s just like the Simultaneous Opposite Cardinal Direction problem used in a fighting game cheat when on a Hitbox, where Hitbox had to add a "scurbber", an electronic circuit to prevent simultaneous actuation to be torunament legal. Now it’s the opposite problem, It’s physically impossible to press 2 opposite cardinals, even though that’s the desired effect for there to be 10 independent, simultaneously active buttons.  Also Track N Field and The Activision Decathlon with the 2600 Track N Field controller improves scores because it de-marries the left and right from being on opposite ends of one axis, letting both left and right be simultaneously pressed.

How do I know? 2600 Space Invaders can be played with that controller.  Try it if you got it.  You don’t need up or down anyway, so why not try it?

They’ve even made third party " 'Asteroids' Button Boxes".  where rotate left, right, thrust, fire, and hyperspace/shield/flip were all on 5 separate buttons.

15659: For those that are so worried about the auto-centering and restricting issues, I have contacted the manufacturer and they have assured me that all of those issues are a mute point. They can make them either way, square or round...centering or not.  so PLEASE quit your whining.
15660:
I designed and built the "Spectre Systems controller". (Which is often referred to as the ICBM Attack controller.) 

 Originally, the pinball buttons on the side were for playing the pinball game with.
 And yes, the 1, 2 and 3 keys were used for the bases.
 

 I was suggesting using 4 pinball buttons for the 3 bases and the start button simply to bring the cost of making a new ICBM Attack controller down. (i.e. dropping the keypad)
 

 One could make a controller with 3 buttons on the top (with the Joystick) to play ICBM Attack, and add two more pinball buttons on the side to play pinball with... 
 

 That design might make the most sense as it would be ergonomically designed to play well with both games.
 

 As to worrying about pushing multiple buttons at the same time, the software will just 'detect' the first button that is pressed that it checks and ignore the others. So that should not be an issue...
 

 If I had a 50K ohm joystick handy, I could build up a prototype in a few hours...
 

 Brett

I just want it the way it was originally designed.  If you mess with it too much, you introduce new problems.  I was just bringing up issues that answer the questions, if the originator of the game and controller was silent, how to best reflect his/her intentions.

 I see the stick is originally a circular restrictor.  Keep it a circular restrictor.   The ICBM Attack program is designed to work with a Circular restrictor.  Let’s stick with that.

Whether it centers or not, make it the way the joystick was originally designed.   I just didn’t know the way it was supposed to be designed.

I just brought up some goofy issues with making things the way it wasn’t designed.  If the original was designed non-centering, the ICBM should be non-centering.   If it was centering, it should be centering.  I never saw it.  I never played with it.  So Bilbrey, was it originally self-centered or not?   Whatever it is, keep it the way it was designed.

If someone wants to make a controller using a keypad or with a square restrictor or with the opposite centering feature of the original, let them  make the controller that way.  It’s going to be a niche item anyway.  So if someone designs a game, that HAS to be with the certain requirements, let the make a controller that way.

I just brought up some points with emulation of older games which ended up being a disaster. Like no paddles on the Xbox One Atari Flashback collections.

Since this is designed to play a historic game, like ICBM Attack, it should be the way it was originally designed, unless the creators didn’t have money or technology at the time to mass produce and do what they want, and would like a do-over, like George Lucas by making Greedo at first shot 2 seconds earlier than Han, and have it gradually reduced to 1 frame, when originally Han shot Greedo under the table, they should have a right to a do-over.   But since this is basically vaporware until it gets made, make it however you want.

(if you bought George Lucas’s reasons for changing the scene and not just because he could and wanted to test the waters of how seemless his revisionism can be.  But he does have a right to do. Tolkein re-wrote The Hobbit which started as just a children’s story, and when he combined elements of it with elements of his Old Testament-like work of Middle Earth, and made basically his epic quest, The Lord of the Rings, which tied them together and resolved everything.  If it’s good enough for Tolkein, it’s good enough for Lucas.)

Spectre should make it the way they want.

I like the idea of a Spectre controller that's as original as possible... but it makes no sense in practice.  A simple, inexpensive-as-possible joystick that can play ICBM Attack is fine with me.  After all, there are no Astrocade games, except for "Attack," that require that controller.


In my mind, original doesn't mean better.  Let's use the Atari 5200's analog controller as an example.  I don't see 5200 users clamoring for exact replacements for their broken controllers.  A 5200 work-alike is much better.  This has come up many times on the 5200 podcast that Glenn is a co-host on.


If I could get it, then I'd prefer a trackball for the Astrocade that could play ICBM Attack.  I just wanna have fun playing original games on real hardware; I'm in no way attached to what type on joystick that I use why I hook up my Astrocade.  That's why I made an Atari-to-Astrocade adapter.  I can use any Atari compatible joystick with my Astrocade.  This doesn't work in cases where the knob and hand controller must be used at the same time (like in Gunfight), but it works in most cases.


Adam

Most trackballs work like a mouse. They are 'delta' positioning, instead of 'absolute' positioning. And a joystick is absolute positioning. 

 Sadly what this means is that a trackball would not work with ICBM Attack as programmed. ICBM Attack would have to be reprogrammed to use a trackball as an input device.
 

 

 Also, ICBM Attack does not use the keypad on the arcade, it uses the keypad on the Spectre Controller.
 

 

 I've been thinking about this for a while now, and if there was a source for a 50K potentiometer, it would be pretty easy to build up a controller that worked with ICBM Attack. Also, I'd throw a couple of extra buttons on the side to also make it play well with the pinball game. When I was building the units, it was a lot more fun playing the pinball game when you were actually pushing pinball buttons.

Aren’t all 10 buttons mapped to either the 2 virtual triggers, or the 8 virtual joypad directions, while the paddles are the 2 axes of the joystick?   I assume the 3 keypad buttons used in ICBM are non-contradictory, (like button 1 doesn’t represent JX(0)=+1 at the same time as Button 2 is JX(0)=-1) I know if you built a controller like that (for example, the Atari Track N Field controller, where left run and right run map to joystick left and joystick right))  Bally Basic and more advanced Bally languages would either…

A)  cancel each other out (+1-1=0) (my first guess)
B)  advance +1 on one line and then -1 on another line and before the frame is finished comes to a net wash of neutral (what I, with my limited knowledge,thing the 2600 does)
C)  not know what to do and go into error
D)  or act unpredictably if Button 1 and 2 are hit simultaneously.

All this is assuming my above (intentionally probably wrong) example is true, because the Bally language thinks of ICBM as a 2 controller game, with individual digital directions and triggers as the 10 buttons.

It’s electronically identical to 2 standard Bally controllers,  but in a more complex 1 player form, and the physical form doesn’t prevent Simultaneous Opposite Cardinal Directions.  The language doesn’t say JN(0)=1 or JS(0)=1, it says JY(0)=1 or JY(0)=-1 with JY(0)=0 being neutral vertically.   It would mess up the Bally if JN(0)=1 and JS(0)=1 simultaneously, which is the physical logic of the handle, but the language treats it as JY(0)= ?????.  There’s nothing in that language for that contingency.

In the original Spectre Controller, the mapping was... 

 Spectre Handle       Basic Variables              Port values
 ------------------       ----------------------       ---------------- 
 X joystick                 KN(1) = -128 to 127      &(28) = 0 to 255
 Y joystick                 KN(2) = -128 to 127      &(29) = 0 to 255
 Left Pinball button   TR(1) = 1                       &(16) = 00010000
 Right Pinball button TR(2) = 1                       &(17) = 00010000
 Keypad - 0               TR(2) = 1                       &(17) = 00010000
 Keypad - 1               JX(2) = -1                      &(17) = 00000100
 Keypad - 2               JY(1) = -1                      &(16) = 00000010
 Keypad - 3               JY(2) = -1                      &(16) = 00000010
 Keypad - 4               JX(1) = -1                      &(16) = 00000100
 Keypad - 5               TR(1) = 1                       &(16) = 00010000
 Keypad - 6               JX(1) = 1                       &(16) = 00001000
 Keypad - 7               JY(2) = 1                       &(17) = 00000001
 Keypad - 8               JY(1) = 1                       &(16) = 00000001
 Keypad - 9               JX(2) = 1                       &(17) = 00001000
 Keypad - S   (I forget where this was wired... if at all...)


 


 As you can see, the keypad 0 key and the right pinball button were wired together, and the keypad 5 key and the left pinball button were wired together.
 

 Also, the port value examples to the right are only if that one function is selected.
 If more than one function is selected on a handle concurrently, then the value in that register would change accordingly.

 


 


 Now, as to what happens when 'conflicting' buttons are pushed at the same time, like key 8 and key 2 (up and down on handle 1).
 

 Actually, what will happen depends on what game it is, and how the bits are being checked.
 And yes, activating more than one 'switch' at a time could be unpredictable...

15672:
I have found where in the cartridge the initial number of balls is set in RAM for Bally Pin.  Normally, you start off with 5 balls.  As far as I can tell, you can't earn any extra balls.  For those who understand Z80 machine language, here is the disassembled and commented code for where the number of "lives" (balls) is set:

$2236  3EFF    	        LD      A,$05            ; Set Initial # of balls
$2238  32CC4F  	        LD      ($4FCC),A        ; Holds Initial # of balls

If you change the $05 to $09, then you'll get 9 balls to start with at the beginning of the game.  Swell, right?  Not quite.  It turns out that if you only change the starting number of balls then your score is scrambled.  Hey, Bob Ogdon (who programmed the game), that's a nice nod to the cheaters among us!  The score is scrambled because elsewhere in the program, Bob checks if the initial number of balls is 5.  If not, then he screws-up the score; it becomes scrambled (I haven't looked into how he does this yet).  So, you also have to change the check for the initial number of balls:

$2BCD  3ACC4F  	        LD      A,($4FCC)
$2BD0  FEFF    	        CP      $05      ; Must match initial # of balls
$2BD2  2002    	        JR      NZ,$2BD6 ;   else the score is messed up!

Here is an example of changing this to nine balls to start with:

$2236  3EFF    	        LD      A,$09            ; Set Initial # of balls
$2238  32CC4F  	        LD      ($4FCC),A        ; Holds Initial # of balls

$2BCD  3ACC4F  	        LD      A,($4FCC)
$2BD0  FEFF    	        CP      $09      ; Must match initial # of balls
$2BD2  2002    	        JR      NZ,$2BD6 ;   else the score is messed up!

This works okay.  If you set the initial number of balls to higher than nine, then the displayed number of balls left on the screen is scrambled for two reasons:

1) The screen space is only meant to hold one digit.

2) I think that the number of lives is held as a BCD number.  If you put a number in above 99, then the display looks weird on the screen.  I've tried $FF, and it DOES work, but then the number of balls displays looks REALLY weird.

So, what this boils down to is this: in order to change the number of lives, use a hex editor to change memory locations in the ROM file to:

Astrocade ROM Cart ROM Space ($2237) is $0237 = Number of Balls
Astrocade ROM Cart ROM Space ($2BD1) is $0BD1 = Number of Balls

To change it to 99 balls, use this:

Astrocade ROM Cart ROM Space ($2237) is $0237 = $99
Astrocade ROM Cart ROM Space ($2BD1) is $0BD1 = $99

Does this make sense?

Go ahead and try it and then try running your game in the MAME emulator.  Let me know if this works for you.

I'm glad that I found this area of RAM so easily, as I am terrible at this game.  I want to get further into the game to check certain parts of the code.

Adam

I did find some limited printer simulators of this type, which seem aimed at the professional market that still uses printers, in many cases grocery stores for printed receipts.  Does anyone know of a printer simulator that could pretend to be an Epson printer or some other printer that was popular with the Astrocade?

George Moses' "Listing Formatter" for Blue Ram BASIC is what was used in the later days of the Arcadian for program printouts. It was setup for a specific printer, but I'm not sure which one.  Does anyone have the details on this?  I think that Michael White had a modified version of the program that worked with his, I think, NEC printer.

Adam
15680:
The original "printing" port was hooked up through the 00 BAUD interface. It was unidirectional. The problem with those at the time is there was no "handshake" capability., so if the printer buffer got full, you would loose data that was still being generated.The Blue RAM Printer port used a 25 pin parallel (Centronics) but it was based on a BASE II printer which was dot matrix, so the control characters would or wouldn't work because all of the printer companies had there own code for non-ASCII characters.All current printers use either a USB port or are wireless. Those are back to serial, but they rely a lot on handshaking.

Long story short, you are better off creating a .WAV file, translating it to a text file and printing it out of your PC.

When Adam and I looked at ways to map the ICBM Attack controller to MAME, I was pleasantly surprised by how well the original ROM played with a trackball mouse.     On Thursday, June 21, 2018, 12:50:52 PM EDT, bilbrey@mac.com [ballyalley] <ballyalley@yahoogroups.com> wrote:

  
Most trackballs work like a mouse. They are 'delta' positioning, instead of 'absolute' positioning. And a joystick is absolute positioning.

Sadly what this means is that a trackball would not work with ICBM Attack as programmed. ICBM Attack would have to be reprogrammed to use a trackball as an input device.

Also, ICBM Attack does not use the keypad on the arcade, it uses the keypad on the Spectre Controller.

I've been thinking about this for a while now, and if there was a source for a 50K potentiometer, it would be pretty easy to build up a controller that worked with ICBM Attack. Also, I'd throw a couple of extra buttons on the side to also make it play well with the pinball game. When I was building the units, it was a lot more fun playing the pinball game when you were actually pushing pinball buttons.

By "cassette," I presume that you're referring to Bally's original use of the term.  That is, "cassette" is a 2KB-8KB cartridge.  Correct?

That is correct. For placing the data in the 0x2000 - 0x3FFF address range. We try to use the bally terms where it makes sense.
 
 >>
Read cassettes and dump them to the SD card
 >>
This would be useful whenever we come across undumped cartridge software (of which there isn't much).

We understand that it's not a super useful thing for most people at this point but it seemed foolish not to add it.
 
 >>
Be a Blueram/Whiteram compatible expansion
 >>

Would you support the 2000-baud tape I/O of the Blue Ram?  This requires an 8154, or FPGA "emulation" of it.

We would actually need more info on how this actually functions. I would love to say no problem but I just don't know at this point.
 
 >>
Save the extended ram to a file on the SD card, allowing you to load it again at a later time
 >>

What would be the main purpose of saving extended RAM?  Would it be saved in plain binary format?  One neat use of it that I can think of is the "easy" creation of BASICarts.  Load an AstroBASIC game into extended RAM, make some adjustments to certain addresses, and then save the data as a plain binary file and use the tape game as a cartridge.

Essentially it is for the extended basics, as you described. Currently the understanding is all the data is actually stored in extended RAM. We have access to every line on the 50 pin expansion connector so if there is some memory that also contains important information it's possible to save it all and place it appropriately when loading. Ideally this would take place of the 2000-baud interface but for backwards compatibility I know it's not the same.
 
 >>
Allow larger games by allowing you to emulate a cassette and preload the extended ram giving you much more space for graphics, code, text, whatever would be needed
 >>

So you could an 8K "cartridge" in the $2000 area and then have up to 48K of continuous RAM in the area starting at (I presume) at $6000.

Again, you've got it. Be able to have your code in 0x2000-0x3FFF and in the extended ram. Loading extended ram data and the cassette/cartridge to really try and remove the limits of memory for user programs.
 
 >>
Balcheck diagnostics with text readout, no more translating hex codes
 >>

Very useful.  Have you reassembled the BalCheck cartridge source code?

With the binaries it's not necessary, it will quite literally emulate the function but auto-translate codes and print to LCD. We also have a real BalCheck unit to test against.

 >>
Balcheck will auto detect your system ROM version
 >>

What does it need to do that for?

There are 2 different versions of the BalCheck software and you need to use the right version for your system ROM. Our BalCheck unit is one with the 2732 ROM with switch for selection based on system ROM.

Allow you to load a version of the system ROM you choose
 >>

This is very useful.  There are some Astrocade users here with early systems that are not compatible with many tape games.

Composite video output with RCA audio output
 >>

Very nice!  I'd love to see my Astrocade videos recorded from a composite source, rather than an RF source.

Powered by an external supply to keep from loading the Bally power supply
 >>

Having an external power supply is great.  It also allows the user to use the 300-baud interface at the same time as the upgrade.

I'm glad these sound good. Removing the block off plate does require opening the system but, and you may know this already, the cassette/cartridge port only feeds the !ROM_CS signal, the data bus, and part of the address bus meaning it isn't feasible to do this with just that port.
 
 >>
I don't know if there are any other additions people might like but I'm open to suggestions
 >>

I'd like to see the ability to bankswitch the cartridge area.  Here is a useful scheme for a 512K bankswitched cartridge:

 http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/bally128k-com/maxflash/Astrocade_Maxflash_512K_Memory_Map.txt http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/bally128k-com/maxflash/Astrocade_Maxflash_512K_Memory_Map.txt

 http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/bally128k-com/maxflash/maxflash.htm http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/bally128k-com/maxflash/maxflash.htm
 

 This is a possibility but is it as useful when you have the extended RAM and the ability to pre-load it? We'll have to do a little more research but a quick look says it doesn't seem impossible. The main constraint would be the MCU RAM. It's only 256K per core, but we could probably come up with something if it really is wanted, or simply limit the size from 512K to 128K-192K as the program and data also resides in the same RAM on the MCU. I personally would rather have 0x2000 - 0x3FFF be fixed and "bank" switch the entire extended ram.
 

How far along are you on this project?
 

 This project was started around February of this year. Many of the functions have been written and functionally proven. The hardware is currently where work is being done. Revision 4 is on it's way from the PCB manufacturer. Once assembled testing will begin again. The new revision has a new MCU to better implement the functions and have a usable and responsive interface. I can't at this time give an ETA since we both have work/family to work around but we hope to post an update soon.
 

 How long have you been an Astrocade user?  Have you just discovered the machine, or are you a longtime fan?

 

 My Dad is definitely a long-time fan of the "retro" machines, including the Astrocade. I find them and the way the were built interesting. For both of us this is a fun and interesting project and it's nice that other people could also have a use for it.

15707:
Brett wrote:
>>
I think [Scott Norris] designed [Music Maker] to help him make music for the games...
>>


Scot did write Music Maker.  This program was meant to be a cartridge for end-users.  The program that Scot wrote to help him write music for Bally cartridges is called Stweek.  Stweek is on most or all of the Astrocade Multicarts, but I couldn't find one video example of this program on YouTube.  The Astrocade FAQ has this to say about Scot's program to create music:

Stweek is a 2K cart.  "This is not a game, it's a "Sound Tweeker" program that gives direct access to the music "registers." It was used as an in-house programming tool to make sound effects and music for other cartridges. A keypad overlay should exist, but it has not turned up yet. Documentation and an overlay would make this
program very useful for home-brewers (and the Astrocade MESS emulation author). Written by Scot L. Norris."

Richard Degler disassembled Stweek in 2008.  He says:

"This program, Sound TWEEKer, which at first glance appears to be a five-line by twenty-character (5 x 20) text editor, is actually a music editor - and also allows direct control of the eight (8) sound registers of the BALLY/Astrocade PROFESSIONAL ARCADE home videogame console."

Richard wrote a manual, created a keypad overlay (two of them, actually), compiled all the notes posted to the Yahoo group about Stweek and included songs saved as MESS save states (These save states are no longer compatible with the current version of MAME).  The two songs he included are "Mountain King" and "Taunt."  The disassembly source code for Stweek (and the aforementioned documentation) is here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/STWEEK_Disassembly_and_More.zip


If you're curious to try Stweek, then the easiest way to load it in MAME under Windows is with this command line, which will make the display look okay (I'm using the debugger version of MAME):

mamed astrocde -cart stweek -debug -nofilter

"Are you curious how to save a song created in Stweek on real hardware?  Sorry, you can't (not without additional RAM, and possibly more hardware).  Here's what Richard wrote about saving from Stweek:

"Actually saving the Music Score is another problem.  I was able to view it with the View Memory window in the MESS debugger, to make sure it matched the original from SONGS (except for the label addresses, of course), but there is no provision to save it.  They must have been using a development machine (most likely CP/M at that time), so it would have been much easier to just use the Music Macros in a cross-assembler.  The result is still the same, and they could have used the Note Names in the original SONGS source, too."


If your curious about Stweek, then it is possible to download an old version of the MESS emulator from 2008 to load the save states.  If anyone does this, it would be useful to upload a video of Stweek to YouTube.  However, you'll find that the cartridge isn't really user-friendly, after all, Scot wrote it for himself.  Yet, thanks to Richard, we now know how to use the program.

Adam
15708:
Here is the history of this cartridge, as I know, it AFTER it left Scot Norris' hands.
Don Gladden (New Image) (I don't know where he got it. It could have been from any of 3 sources. 1) George Moses or 2) Dave Carson (who had an uncanny way of getting things before the internet) or 3) someone else?!?
Then Leroy Flamm got a copy from Don at the ASTROBASH in Michigan. He was talking to Mike White through open windows of their cars and said to Mike something about he would like to be able to save the data but didn't know how to do that. Mike reached into his back seat and grabbed a new AstroBASIC cartridge and said "here, there is all of the amplifier and I/O you should need." A couple of months later, Leroy had the finished cart. The keypad overlay and instructions and label were all done by Mike White, as well as the box it was shipped in. Thus that cart was a hybrid of the Scot Norris' STWEEK and an AstroBASIC's I/O system combined by the late Leroy Flamm and finishing touches by Mike White.Ken

15710:
I found a guy on Atari Age, nurmix, who makes INTV Flashback control to INTV 1 and INTV 2 console adapters.   The INTV 1s require opening your system, but nothing shocking, as I can attest to.

He said he now makes one-by-one 9-pin to 9-pin adapters.  Here’s his conversation:  http://atariage.com/forums/topic/237113-intellivision-flashback-controller-adapters-round-2/

I’ve suggested a couple I want. The2 that would most intersest the astrocade community is the Atari Control-> Bally Machine adapter and the Bally Control  ->  Atari Machine adapter.  I gave him the glankonian web page ith the pin adapters

Also of interest to the community who wants to play Astrocade games with a2600 stick, but want it left, a lefty adapter.

When I righthand certain games, like Tutankham, Pac-Land, and Sidearms, using a Beeshu controller is reversed buttons, so it it’s just a simple mechanical swap of pins, then a Button flipper would be good too.  Also would come in handy to someone for a 5200 Competition Pro controller for right main fire.

Finally, according to that same web page, it looks like the Astrocade "thinks" in terms of component hookups, aka Y/Pb/Pr. Why settle for an S-Video mod when you can get a component mod?  Isn’t it easier just tot route the Luma to Green, the Pb to Blue and the Pr to Red than to combine the Pb and Pr into a C for a Y/C connection?  The answer is because component CRT TVs are expensive.   But if you’ve got one, why not?

te website I’m talking about is http://www.glankonian.com/~lance/Hack.html

15712:
I meant Green as in the color of cable, not green a a variable where 0%=un-green  (which is black if R and B are both 0, Or any various color along the Red-Blue swath with the most ungreen color being Magenta if R=100% and B=100%.) and 100%=green.   In tv hookups, if it’s Y/Cb/Cr then the green cable is the Y or black and white signal, Pb is B-Y and is usually hooked up to a Blue cable, and Pr is R-Y and is usually hooked up with a red cable.

Ever hook up a PS2, Xbox Orginal, Game Cube, or Wii with the best authorized default hookup?  That’s Y/Cb/Cr if analog, or Y/Pb/Pr if digital.

By the way is there a difference between Cb and Pb or between Cr and Pr)

Most TVs at around 2000 and beyond are built for Y/Cb/Cr connections.  It will even work on a modern TV, (but if you use a modern TV, I’ll beat you in Space Fortress or that one Bally Basic game that is like it, because I will use a CRT TV and get the ping advantage.)  Footage:  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OscmOzEitkI&t=6s

The red green and blue cables that come with those mentioned consoles?   They are NOT RGB.  They Y/Cb/Cr, so a lot of factory off the shelf wires have a 480i Y/Cb/Cr mode.  My point is if you have a TV for one of those systems, and they have a set of Y/Cb/Cr/L/R plugs on their TV, then the Astrocade will have millions of colors, or at least as many as it can process up to that millions.  And CRT TV are analog technology, even though they only have 480 points per line, the CTR TV does a good jobs of blending the colors to the point of, what Laser Discs enthusiasts say, if it were digitized accurately, it would be 90 bit color.   Compared to 36 bit color of HDR on digital sets of high end TVs today. And what the nature of bits, adding one bits doubles the number of possible colors.

Every system between the PS2, Xbox Original, Game Cube, 360, Wii, PS3 and Wii U had analog options.   And every system before that was purely analog.  What do I miss on those TV I can’t get with modern ones?  Those ping-free reaction times.  There’s never been a greater ping test than 2600 Kaboom.

I wrote these notes for myself this morning, since it took me a while (too long!) to remember how to clean a non-BASIC WAV file.  I thought that the notes might be useful for other people, so I cleaned them up a little and I'm posting them here.  This document presumes that you're familiar with process of archiving Astrocade programs already.  If not, then I advise you to try archiving an "AstroBASIC" program first and then come back to this document.

Cleaning a RAW Binary (Non-BASIC) WAV file with BallyBin and AstroWAV
By Adam Trionfo
Version 1.0
July 10, 2018

Summary:

These are general instructions, written mostly so that I'll remember the process, on how to clean an Astrocade's RAW 2000-baud binary recording created with the Blue Ram Utility.

I used the tape version of the Blue Ram Utility 3 by Perkins Engineering.  I loaded the utility from a WAV file into my Blue Ram 16K unit.  In this example, I converted the 2KB Machine Language Manager (MLM) cartridge by Bit Fiddlers to a WAV file that can be loaded with "AstroBASIC."

Here are the steps to load the Blue Ram Utility:

Load the Blue Ram Utility using Blue Ram BASIC using :INPUT.  (Do not try to load it using :INPUT %(24576).  This will not work.)

2) The version of the utility that I used is in the file:

Blue RAM Utility (Perkins Engineering).zip

This file is located here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/ram_expansion_required/perkins_engineering/Blue%20RAM%20Utility%20(Perkins%20Engineering).zip

The file contains a zip file called Blue RAM Utility and Instructions (1982)(Perkins Engineering)(2000 baud)(Blue RAM BASIC).zip

The Blue RAM Utility files in that zip file are called:

1) Blue RAM Utility (1982)(Perkins Engineering)(2000 baud)(Blue RAM BASIC)(Load 1 of 2).wav

2) Blue RAM Utility (1982)(Perkins Engineering)(2000 baud)(Blue RAM BASIC)(Load 2 of 2).wav

3) Blue RAM Utility Instructions (1982)(Perkins Engineering)(2000 baud)(Blue RAM Utility).wav

Load loads 1 and 2 one after the other into BRB.  The program will run automatically after using :INPUT.

My intent was to create a loadable WAV file of the Machine Language Manager cartridge.  First, I loaded the Machine Language Manager cartridge into the Blue Ram Utility using the COPY command.

Then I verified that the load was correct using VRFY.

After that, I saved the 2KB MLM program to a "tape" (WAV file) using the Utility's SAVE command.  I will not go into details about how I did the above steps.  It's easy once you know how, but is beyond the scope of this document.  If you are curious about how it's done, then the detailed instructions for how to use the Blue Ram Utility are available online here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/perkins/docs-blue_ram_utility3.pdf

After I had a RAW WAV file on my computer that was output from the Utility, I used Audacity to amplify the file.  I saved this amplified file and then used Ballybin 2 on the WAV to digitally archive the file.

Here are the general steps on how to clean a non-BASIC binary file saved in the Astrocade's 2000-baud WAV format using Ballybin and AstroWAV 2.

First, there are two versions of BallyBin and AstroWAV 2.  Make sure to use the following version of these two files:

AstroWAV and Ballybin 2 (2004)(Bob Colbert)(beta)[Feb 27 2004]

Once you have these files on your Windows PC, use the command line to clean the saved RAW WAV file.  It is presumed here that the RAW WAV file is called input.wav.  First create a BML file of the RAW file using the following command:

ballybin -l3 -v2 -i1 -bcleaned input.wav

Next, make a cleaned WAV file:

astrowav -h3 -f1 -woutput.wav cleaned.bml

This WAV file is stereo.  I used Audacity to make it mono, but this step isn't required.

This cleaned WAV file can be loaded into an Astrocade with expansion RAM by following these steps:

1) Insert "AstroBASIC" into Astrocade.

2) Make sure that you're Astrocade RAM expansion has the switches in the 6K area and is set to RAM.

3) In "AstroBASIC," type: :INPUT %(24576)

4) When the program is done loading, hold down Reset and keep it down.  Switch the RAM expansion switches to 2K and ROM.  Then release the Reset button.

After releasing the Reset button, the cartridge (which was saved as a WAV file) should load perfectly.  The "AstroBASIC" cartridge which is in the slot will be ignored.

[End of Document]

Ken left me a message on how to run the Blue Ram Utility from the UltiMulti cartridge rather than running it from tape.  I've done that before, but in this particular case, I wanted to run the utility from tape.  In the end, I wanted to use the Machine Language Manager (MLM) cartridge as an machine language monitor while going through some examples in a Z80 programming book.


The MLM is quite useful for real-time assembly work on the Amiga.  Enter a short ML subroutine using hex, execute it, and then see the results in RAM and the registers.  Pretty cool! For real-time work, the MLM can't be beat on the Astrocade.


The best way to develop ML programs that don't require real-time use on the Astrocade is the Blue Ram Utility.  It's simply wonderful, but time has passed it by long ago.  Now, programming the Astrocade is best done on other systems.  For current Astrocade programming projects, I wouldn't give up the Zmac Z80 cross-assembler/HVGLIB/ MAME combination.


Adam

Here is some information about the cartridge and the video:

Machine Language Manager (MLM) is a 2KB cartridge written by Andy Guevara in 1981 for the Bally Arcade/Astrocade.  It was released by The Bit Fiddlers in late 1981/early 1982.

This video overview summarizes the Machine Language Manager cartridge.  This program is a machine language monitor which allows direct access to programming the Z80 CPU.  This cartridge does not require extra memory to use it, but it can take advantage of extra RAM if it is available.

"The Bally/Astrocade Game Cartridge and Hardware FAQ" says this about the MLM:

"This cartridge, which included [a 24-key keypad] overlay, provides an "easy" way to program the Astrocade in machine language. Though not a Z-80 assembler, MLM does simplify the entry of hex code (which otherwise must be entered using decimal via BASIC. Also, the keypad layout does not require the use of the key-shifts, so typing is faster). Programs can be saved via the Bally BASIC 300-baud interface (later, subroutines were written that allowed the 2000 baud version of Bally BASIC (#6004) to be swapped out for tape saving). "Machine Language Manager" does NOT have a built-in cassette interface."

This overview is part one of a four part series.  The series includes:

1) Machine Language Manager, Part 1: Overview and Background
2) Machine Language Manager, Part 2: How to Use the MLM
3) Machine Language Manager, Part 3: Using MLM Example Programs
4) Machine Language Manager, Part 4: Using MLM with the Astrocade MAME Emulation

This video is split into several parts:

0:00 - MLM Titles
0:30 - Short Introduction to the MLM
3:11 - Overview with Cart, Overlay and Interface
3:32 - Close-Up of MLM and Overlay
4:38 - Closer Close-Up of MLM and Overlay
5:52 - Extreme Close-Up of MLM and Overlay
6:57 - Introduction and History of the MLM
23:25 - MLM Cart, Documentation and Overlay
24:39 - MLM Manual
26:26 - Saving/Loading at 2000-Baud
28:05 - Goldfish Demo Source Code
29:33 - Bound Astrocade Machine Language Book
33:04 - Overview of Three Z80 Programming Books
34:09 - Overview of Programming the Z80, by Rodnay Zaks
36:20 - Overview of Z80 Software Gourmet Guide and Cookbook, by Nat Wadsworth
37:46 - Overview of Software and Hardware for the Bally Arcade - A Technical Description (aka, the "Nutting Manual")
40:25 - Z80 CPU Microprocessor Instant Reference Card
41:33 - Creating a 24-Key Keypad Overlay for the MLM
45:30 - End Credits

This video is aimed at someone who has little or no understanding of Z80 machine language.  A Z80 machine language programming novice, or anyone who has a passing interest in using the Machine Language Manager cartridge, will get more out of it if all of the four videos in this series are watched one after the other.  Also, even if you have no plans to ever use the Machine Language Manager cartridge, anyone who wanted to know how to program the Astrocade will find plenty of general information provided in this video.

Enjoy!

Hi all, as part of an ongoing effort to document the history of the early video game scene in the US, I've been trying to track down release dates as accurately as possible for classic consoles. In the case of the Astrocade, this has manifested in using the handful of months provided mainly out of the Computer Entertainer/Video Game Update industry newsletter, and the ads and news from the Arcadian newsletter scans (as well as a little bit of information from the Weekly Television Digest industry periodicals I've got access to). So far this is what I've got - 1978 is really messy, so any clarification there would be lovely! Anything bold is something I'm pretty confident in.

1978: (9 releases)

Last 2 weeks of Dec 77 into January - System started shipping after orders started coming in fall of 77, launched w/ dealer democart and 3 others + 3 more later in Jan? (from tv digest 12-26-77)

January: Dealer Democart (sold broadly in 83 via arcadian),

May: Baseball/Tennis, Elementary Math (advertised as launch games in 9-19-77 tv digest, but Arcadian notes on shelves in May issue)

August: Sea Wolf? (or earlier)

Early Fall?: 280 Zzzap, Panzer Attack,

October: Tiny BASIC (Arcadian 2-1)

Late Fall?: Clowns/Brickyard, Blackjack/Poker


1979: (6 releases)

January:  Amazing Maze(Arcadian 1-03, though advertised as being available in the fall in volume 00), Football (Late Dec to early Jan)

February: Star Battle (Arcadian 1-05)

October: Bally Pinball (rereleased 1981 as Astrocade Pinball), Space Invaders (later Astro Battle w/ Astrocade) - 1-11 arcadian

?: Letter Match (by august via ad in 1-09 arcadian),


1980: (1 release) - Bally announces sale of home division at Jan CES to Fidelity Electronics (1-14-80 TV Digest) sale falls through in March (arcadian); Astrovision agrees to buy August

October: Dog Patch(last Bally labeled release),


1981:(7 releases, 2 of them homebrew)

August: Galaxian(Galactic Invasion) - Arcadian 3-10

September: Biorhythm, Grand Prix/Demolition Derby, Astrovision BASIC (Arcadian 3-12)

October: Space Fortress (arcadian 3-12, def out by Jan CES)

November: Blue RAM Extended BASIC (4-1 arcadian)

December: Machine Language Manager (Arcadian 4-2)


1982: (5 brand new releases, 2 3rd party/homebrew)

March: Galactic Invasion? (Galaxian in 1981, 4-4 arcadian indicates was available by jan ces)

May: Blue Ram 8K Extended BASIC (Arcadian 4-7)

August: Incredible Wizard

September: Pirate’s Chase

October: Artillery Duel,

?: ICBM Attack (Mentioned arcadian 4-9, July issue)


1983: (8 releases, 6 3rd party/homebrew)

March 6: Muncher (5-5 Arcadian, orders opened Jan - technically unofficial unreleased Pac-Man game)

April: Treasure Cove(May in CE? But April in Arcadian 5-6)

July: Blast Droids (Arcadian 5-9)

August: Solar Conqueror(Sept 83?), Cosmic Raiders (Arcadian 5-10)

September: Ms. Candy Man(Arcadian 5-11)

Sept. 24: Sneaky Snake

December: Sea Devil (Ad Arcadian 6-2)


1984: (1 release, homebrew/3rd party)

March: Maze Man (ad in Arcadian 6-5)


1985:(9 releases, all homebrew releases of prototypes or third party games)

May: Life (Ad in Arcadian 7-1)

December: Soccer, Bowling, Checkers, Conan, Music Maker (Arcadian 7-2), also available are Songs (by Moses), Video Story Book, Missile Attack(ICBM modded for standard controls)


Unreleased/prototype: Drag Race, Chess, Creative Crayon

15733:
Be sure to distinguish the two different demo carts--the 4K Dealer Demo, which features the built-in software, and the 8K Bally BASIC demo, which is a modified version of BASIC plus a sample program. Both are from 1978, but I'd imagine the BASIC demo came later since BASIC didn't launch with the system.
 

 I don't think "Tiny BASIC" was ever used as an official name, though it was based on that. Technically, I think both versions are labeled "Bally BASIC", though we tend to refer to the later release with the 2000 baud interface as "AstroBASIC".
 

 If you really want to go down a rabbit hole, you can start looking through the documents from Bob Fabris, the editor of The Arcadian. Sometimes people even wrote him letters talking about the games they'd just bought. Bally Alley is really just scratching the surface of those. You might find some additional ones on the Internet Archive, though not all of them yet.
 

 https://archive.org/details/ballyalley&tab=collection https://archive.org/details/ballyalley&tab=collection
 

 We've talked to a lot of people involved with the system, though certainly not all. I could talk to you about it more privately if you want.
 

 Paul (AKA ranger_lennier on AtariAge)

Here is some information about the cartridge and the video:

Machine Language Manager (MLM) is a 2KB cartridge written by Andy Guevara in 1981 for the Bally Arcade/Astrocade.  It was released by The Bit Fiddlers in late 1981/early 1982.

This video explains how to use the Machine Language Manager cartridge, a machine language monitor that allows direct access to programming the Z80 CPU.  This cartridge does not require extra memory to use it, but it can take advantage of extra RAM if it is available.

This overview is part two of a four part series.  The series includes:

1) Machine Language Manager, Part 1: Overview and Background
2) Machine Language Manager, Part 2: How to Use the MLM
3) Machine Language Manager, Part 3: Using MLM Example Programs
4) Machine Language Manager, Part 4: Using MLM with the Astrocade MAME Emulation

This video is split into several parts:

0:0:00 - "How to Use the MLM" Titles
0:0:15 - Short Introduction to the MLM Video Series
0:0:44 - Overview of the MLM Manual
0:13:00 - Using the MLM: Section 1

- What is the MLM
- The Start-Up Screen
- Usable RAM vs. Lines Per Screen
- MLM Keypad Overlay
- MLM Commands: ADDR., WRITE, READ and LIST

0:23:27 - Using the MLM: Section 2

- Examining ASCII Text in ROM
- Changing MLM Defaults
- Debugging a "Program"
- MLM Command: REG.

0:43:03 - Using the MLM: Section 3

- Using the MLM Assembly Listing
- Using a SYSTEM Routine
- Using RECTAN
- Typing in Example 5-1
- A Splash of Green

0:49:31 - Using the MLM: Section 4

- The User Program Interface (UPI)
- FILL (Subroutine $1A)

1:00:00 - Using the MLM: Section 5

The User Program Interface (UPI)

- MOVE (Subroutine $5E)
- (aka Copy)

1:07:12 - Using the MLM: Section 6

- An MLM Single Byte CALL
- STRING (Print String)

1:24:20 - Using the MLM: Section 7

- Saving an ML Program with the 300-Baud Tape Interface
- No Tapes; Using WAV Files
- Saving/Loading a Program
- Checking a Program
- Running a Program

1:35:39 - MLM: Wrap-Up and Preview of Parts 3 and 4
1:36:48 - End Credits

This video is aimed at someone who has little or no understanding of Z80 machine language.  A Z80 machine language programming novice, or anyone who has a passing interest in using the Machine Language Manager cartridge, will get more out of it if all of the four videos in this series are watched one after the other.  Also, even if you have no plans to ever use the Machine Language Manager cartridge, anyone who wanted to know how to program the Astrocade will find plenty of general information provided in this video.

Enjoy!

Adam

Dave asked:
>>
Does anyone have a list of games that do not use the knob at all in gameplay?
>>

I have not seen a list of Astrocade games that don't use the knob.  It would be much easier to write a list of the games that don't use the knob.

Note that most (possibly all?) cartridge games can use the knob for input to menus (for selection of lives, difficulty, etc).  This is called "Remote selection."  The menus always allow input from the keypad.

Some of the games that require the knob are:

280 Zzzap / Dodgem
Clowns / Brickyard
Conan The Barbarian
Dogpatch
Gunfight / Scribbling
Music Maker
Soccer / Dribbling
Tornado Baseball / Tennis / Hockey / Handball
War

I'm not sure if this list is complete, but I know it covers nearly all of the knob games.  There may be some less-popular/education titles that I didn't list.  Am I missing any games that require the knob on this list?

Adam

This 44:04 minute video shows five example programs for use with the Machine Language Manager cartridge.  This is video 3 of 4 of the MLM series.

Machine Language Manager (MLM) is a 2KB cartridge written by Andy Guevara in 1981 for the Bally Arcade/Astrocade. It was released by The Bit Fiddlers in late...


You can download or stream the 1.06GB mp4 file from archive.org:


https://archive.org/details/MLMbyBiFiddlersPart3MLMExamplePrograms


The five machine language programs are:

1) Critter, by Brett Bilbrey - Display and move a Space Invader-like creature.  Knob #1 controls its speed.

2) Standard Color Generator, by Andy Guevara - Generates eight standard color used in TV work.

3) 256 Color Program, by Jerry Burianyk - Displays 256 colors on-screen at one time.  Knob #1 controls how many colors are displayed onscreen at once.

4) ASCII Character Set, by Andy Guevara - Prints the entire MM 3x5-pixel character set.

5) Goldfish Demo, by Andy Guevara - Displays seven fish in an aquarium with a cat in the background.  A clock displays the time in H:M:S format.  The cat meows once a minute.

The first four programs were included as machine language listing with comments in the MLM user manual.  The last program, Goldfish Demo, was available on tape and as a separate Z80 ML listing.  There is background and source material about each program.  The programs are loaded using the 300-baud tape interface.

The five machine language program examples included in this video make up part three of a four part series.  The series includes:

1) Machine Language Manager, Part 1: Overview and Background
2) Machine Language Manager, Part 2: How to Use the MLM
3) Machine Language Manager, Part 3: Using MLM Example Programs
4) Machine Language Manager, Part 4: Using MLM with the Astrocade MAME Emulation

This video is split into several parts:

0:00 - "Using MLM Example Programs" Titles
0:02 - Overview of Video
1:43 - Program 1: Critter
7:23 - Program 2: Standard Color Generator
10:49 - Program 3: 256 Color Program
18:07 - Program 4: ASCII Character Set
23:25 - Program 5: Goldfish Demo
41:08 - MLM: Wrap-Up and Preview of Part 4
43:48 - End Credits


This video series is aimed at someone who has little or no understanding of Z80 machine language.  This video, in particular, can be enjoyed by anyone, whether or not they have any interest in machine language at all.  A Z80 machine language programming novice, or anyone who has a passing interest in using the Machine Language Manager cartridge, will get more out of it if all of the four videos in this series are watched one after the other.


Enjoy!
